purpose: Additional individually selected explanatory footnotes in Simanim 60 through the end of Tzidkat HaTzadik. Existing notes and source text are preserved. Selected connections do not certify an exhaustive review of every siman.
method: Complete originating discussions and selected target contexts reviewed; exact contiguous source thoughts, English translations, argument-specific explanations and placement checked in a second reading. No reciprocal placement is approved by these records.

records.originEnglish: Therefore, a person must be vigilant that he himself remains completely clear in this, as it is written: "And I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu" (Hosea 1:4), and likewise regarding Baasha, see Rashi there; and therefore it is said: "Gather yourselves together and assemble"—first adorn yourself and only then adorn others (Bava Metzia 107b), for otherwise one is punished for doing so.
records.targetHebrew: וזה, כי תבנה בית חדש ועשית מעקה לגגך, שצריך האדם לראות שעל ידי עבודתו לא יפול מי לארץ, ורק יתן מקום לכל בריה, וזה מורה מצות מעקה:
records.targetEnglish: This is the meaning of ‘When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof’: a person must see to it that no one falls to the ground through his service. Rather, he must make room for every creature; this is what the commandment of the parapet teaches.
records.themeTitle: A safeguard against harming others through one's own service
records.themeSummary: Rebuking another does not exempt the rebuker from examining his own conduct and the harm he may cause.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef extends the parapet beyond physical construction to responsibility for the effects of one's avodah on another person. This sharpens Rav Tzadok's demand to correct oneself before correcting others: even an act presented as religious service needs a safeguard against causing another person's fall. The other's need for correction does not by itself justify the manner of rebuke.

records.originEnglish: The priests are termed "holy," as it is written: "And Aaron was set apart, that he should be sanctified" (I Chronicles 23:13), and it is said: "even him whom He has chosen will He cause to come near unto Him" (Numbers 16:5). records.targetEnglish: for Aharon, peace be upon him, was separated from Israel "to sanctify him as most holy" (I Divrei HaYamim 23:13); within whom resided the ultimate manifestation of holiness and separation achievable in this world; wherefore he alone entered the Holy of Holies, the place concerning which it is written: "And there shall be no man in the tent of meeting when he goes in to make atonement" (Vayikra 16:17); which the Sages expounded in the Jerusalem Talmud (Yoma 1:5): "even the angels whose faces have the likeness of a man"; for there exists a holiness transcending the angels which they cannot reach, reserved for the righteous whose partition is set inside the ministering angels. And Israel is "one nation in the earth" (II Shmuel 7:23), all forming a single complete corporate stature; except that just as within the human body there are primary vital organs containing greater life-force, like the heart which is the wellspring of vitality; and so other organs exist in descending rungs: organs upon which life directly depends, like the brain and lungs; and organs upon which less vitality depends, like the liver which is kosher if perforated and does not render treifah save if removed entirely leaving less than an olive's volume at the gallbladder (Chullin 46a); and organs whose total removal does not extinguish life, only causing illness, like the kidneys (Chullin 54a); and parts that do not touch vitality at all, yet their injury causes severe bodily pain and illness; and parts where injury causes only minor and brief pain, like bruises on the external surface of the body; and parts that feel no pain whatsoever, being like superfluities, such as fingernails and hair, possessing various descending rungs; yet all are an integral part of the complete stature, the fingernail being called a human fingernail, part of the person's body; all receiving vitality from the heart, whence flow the issues of life (Mishlei 4:23); and according to the vitality channeled from the heart, so is the life of all organs and the collective stature!
records.themeTitle: Aharon's holiness within Israel's shared life
records.themeSummary: The priestly distinction is an enduring root whose revelation varies in degree.
records.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim develops the comparison to a single body: Aharon's concentrated holiness serves a people whose different members receive life in different measures. This explains why the siman can affirm a real priestly root even where its outward expression is slight. Difference of function and degree need not mean a separate source of life.

records.originHebrew: אֲבָל הַגֵּרִים אִי אֶפְשָׁר לָהֶם לִזְכּוֹת לְמַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל כֵּיוָן שֶׁאֵינוֹ מִזַּרְעוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב, רַק כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (אָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן פֶּרֶק לו) עַל פָּסוּק "וּבְשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכַנֶּה" – אֵלּוּ גֵּרֵי הַצֶּדֶק, שֶׁהוּא רַק כְּמוֹ כִּנּוּי וְלֹא עֶצֶם הַשֵּׁם.
records.originEnglish: yet converts cannot achieve the essential biological level of Israel since they do not descend from Jacob's seed, rather as our Sages expounded (Avot DeRabbi Natan 36) on the verse "and surname himself by the name of Israel" (Isaiah 44:5)—these are righteous converts, meaning that it is merely an adopted surname and appellation, and not the intrinsic, inherited name itself.
records.targetHebrew: [שֶׁגַּם הַגֵּרִים הַנִּלְוִים עַל בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָאִים בַּכָּתוּב: "וּבְשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכַנֶּה", וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: אֵלּוּ הַגֵּרִים וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁהָרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ אָמְרָה "וּבְשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכַנֶּה", מִסְּתָמָא יִתְכַּנֶּה בֶּאֱמֶת כֵּן, אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ דַּם הָעֶצֶם בְּתוֹלָדָה, רַק כִּנּוּי שֶׁהוּא שֵׁם הַמִּתְחַדֵּשׁ לָאָדָם אַחַר כָּךְ עַל יְדֵי פְּעֻלּוֹתָיו אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא מְכֻנֶּה כָּךְ, וְגַם אִיתָא בִּיחֶזְקֵאל שֶׁהַגֵּר יִהְיֶה נַחֲלָתוֹ בְּנַחֲלַת הַשֵּׁבֶט שֶׁיִּהְיֶה, הֲרֵי שֶׁהוּא נִכְלָל תּוֹךְ הַשֵּׁבֶט, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]:
records.targetEnglish: for even converts joined to Israel are designated by Scripture: "and surname himself by the name of Israel" (Isaiah 44:5), expounded by our Sages as referring to sincere converts. And since the Holy Spirit declared "shall surname himself by the name of Israel," he is truly so designated, though not by natural biological lineage but through an acquired title earned through righteous actions. Nonetheless he is designated thus, and Ezekiel (47:23) foretells that the convert shall receive an inheritance within the tribe where he sojourns, subsumed within the tribe; and this is not its place.
records.themeTitle: An acquired name that is nevertheless true
records.themeSummary: The distinction between inherited spiritual roots and an acquired name requires Rav Tzadok's own qualification concerning converts.
records.explanation: Dover Tzedek addresses the same expression, ‘by the name of Israel,’ and insists that Scripture's naming of converts is true; he also invokes their inclusion in a tribe's inheritance. This guards the present siman's terminology from being mistaken for a denial of the convert's actual inclusion in Israel. His distinction concerns the manner in which the name is received, through birth or subsequent attachment.

records.originEnglish: And this is the inner meaning of falling upon one's face (nefilat apayim / Tachanun) following each prayer, for the Zohar states at the beginning of Parashat Korach that falling on one's face represents the surrender of oneself unto death, and even in its literal posture it hints at this. And Moses and Aaron fell upon their faces twice there in Parashat Korach.
records.targetHebrew: וזה ענין שאמרו כאן אל אלהי הרוחות לכל בשר, וכמו שאיתא בזוה"ק (שם) ת"ח משה ואהרן מסרו גרמייהו למיתה, שזה המסירות נפש היה בירור על כל הכלל ישראל, ששורש חיותם מקבלים ממקום גבוה שהוא למעלה מן חטאם (עיין שם בזוה"ק היטב). וזה ענין שנזכר כאן לכל בשר, וכמו שאמר כבוד אזמו"ר זללה"ה שזה מרמז כמו שכתוב (תהילים ע״ח:ל״ט) ויזכור כי בשר המה רוח הולך ולא ישוב, והיינו שזה ענין הזכרה לטובה, שהשי"ת חס על האדם מפני שהוא רק בשר. וזה ענין שהזכיר משרע"ה כאן זה, שהתפלל להשי"ת שיעורר ממקום הזה ולא ידח מן כל העדה נדח.
records.targetEnglish: This is the meaning of the words spoken here, ‘God, God of the spirits of all flesh.’ As the holy Zohar says there, Moses and Aharon surrendered themselves to death: this surrender disclosed the truth concerning all Israel, whose root of vitality they receive from a high place above their sin; examine the Zohar there carefully. This is why ‘all flesh’ is mentioned here. As my holy grandfather explained, it alludes to ‘He remembered that they were flesh, a wind that passes and does not return.’ This is remembrance for good: Hashem has compassion on a person because he is only flesh. Moses mentioned this here in praying that Hashem awaken mercy from this place, so that none of the congregation be cast away.
records.themeTitle: Surrender that becomes a plea for the community
records.themeSummary: Moshe and Aharon's falling on their faces is part of their intercession for Israel.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef reads the same Zohar passage as an appeal to the root of Israel's life that lies beyond its failure. This makes the direction of their surrender clear: it becomes a prayer that the congregation be preserved. Their willingness to relinquish their own standing is joined to compassion for others, rather than a claim of personal superiority over those who sinned.

records.originHebrew: סו] תְּפִלָּה צָרִיךְ לְכָל דָּבָר, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּגְזַר מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ. הֲלֹא תִרְאֶה בְּאֵלִיָּהוּ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ ה': "הֵרָאֵה אֶל אַחְאָב וְאֶתְּנָה מָטָר" (מְלָכִים א יח, א), וְאַף עַל פִּי כֵן נֶאֱמַר אַחַר כָּךְ שֶׁעָלָה לְרֹאשׁ הַכַּרְמֶל "וַיִּגְהַר וְגוֹמֵר", שֶׁהִרְבָּה בִּתְפִלָּה עַד שֶׁבָּא גֶּשֶׁם.
records.originEnglish: Prayer is required for every matter, even when it has already been decreed by the Blessed Name. Behold, consider Elijah, to whom Hashem explicitly promised: "Go, show yourself to Ahab, and I will send rain" (I Kings 18:1); and nonetheless it is related afterward that he ascended to the top of Carmel, "and bowed himself down, etc." (ibid. 18:42), praying intensely until the rain arrived.
records.targetHebrew: והבין מזה שסיבב לו השי"ת מעשה כזאת, שהרצון של השי"ת הוא שיתפלל בעד כל הדור שיחזרו בתשובה, כדי שיהיה מטר אחר שהרעב התגבר כ"כ, לזה היה חפץ השי"ת שיתפלל אליהו בעד כל הדור שיחזרו בתשובה, כי לא יחפוץ השי"ת במות הרשע כי אם בשובו מדרכיו וחיה.
records.targetEnglish: He understood from this that Hashem had brought such an event about for him because Hashem's will was that he pray for the entire generation to return in repentance, so that rain might come after the famine had grown so severe. Hashem therefore desired that Elijah pray for the whole generation to repent, for Hashem does not desire the wicked person's death, but rather that he return from his ways and live.
records.themeTitle: The promised rain still calls for prayer
records.themeSummary: Prayer participates in the fulfillment of the promised good rather than merely supplying information about the need.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains Elijah's experience as a summons to pray for his generation's return. The rain is therefore connected with a change in the relationship between the people and Hashem. This illuminates why the promise cited here does not make Elijah's prayer redundant: the prayer itself belongs to the path by which the promised mercy is received.

records.originHebrew: וְעַל זֶה אָמַר: "וְאַחַר הָרוּחַ רַעַשׁ – לֹא בָרַעַשׁ ה', וְאַחַר הָרַעַשׁ אֵשׁ וְגוֹמֵר" (מְלָכִים א יט, יא–יב), כִּי כְּבוֹד ה' אֵינוֹ בְּדָבָר הַנִּרְגָּשׁ וּמַרְעִישׁ, רַק "בְּקוֹל דְּמָמָה דַקָּה", וְהוּא הַלֵּב שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִרְגָּשׁ לְשׁוּם בְּרִיָּה.
records.originEnglish: And regarding this Scripture states: "and after the wind an earthquake, but Hashem was not in the earthquake; and after the earthquake a fire, etc." (I Kings 19:11–12), for the glory of Hashem is not found in sensational, noisy display, but in "a still small voice," which is the inward heart, unfelt and unseen by any created being.
records.targetHebrew: וזה שאומרים מקודם חדו חצדי חקלא שהוא רק הכנה לכנוס בהקדושה נצרך להיות בדבור ובקלא. ואח"כ קדם רבון עלמין היינו כשמגיעין ועומדין לפניו ית"ש ממש אז ולאו מלתא אוושא. כי ענין רוח רעש אש שקודם הקול דממה דקה הם הכנה לשורש היחוד והדביקות בה' אחד.
records.targetEnglish: This is why we first say, ‘Rejoice, reapers of the field’: since this is only preparation for entering holiness, speech and sound are needed. Afterward comes ‘before the Master of worlds’: when one reaches the point of actually standing before Him, blessed be His name, then ‘it is not a matter of noise.’ The wind, earthquake, and fire that precede the still, thin voice are preparation for the root of unity and attachment to the one God.
records.themeTitle: The noise prepares for a quieter attainment
records.themeSummary: Struggle and energetic practice can prepare the heart without being the final form of its attachment.
records.explanation: In Nitzavim, Rav Tzadok applies the same sequence of wind, earthquake, fire, and stillness to entering Shabbos. The distinction is between preparation and attained closeness, not between worthwhile and worthless effort. It helps explain both halves of this siman: the initial struggle is necessary, while settled mastery is recognized by the heart's quieter attachment.

records.originHebrew: וְזֶהוּ פָּרָה אֲדֻמָּה] לְטַהֵר מִטֻּמְאַת מֵת, וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה חֻקַּת): תָּבֹא אֵם וּתְקַנַּח צוֹאַת בְּנָהּ;
records.originEnglish: And this is the red heifer (Parah Adumah) designed to purify from the defilement of death, and our Sages expounded (Bemidbar Rabbah, Chukat 19:8): "Let the mother come and wipe away the excrement of her son";
records.targetHebrew: ולפיכך כשממשיך מרזא דחכמתא ושם לא שייך שום העדר, ממילא מכיר גם הוא שבישראל לא שייך שום העדר החיים. ולזה כתיב קודם טהרת הפרה ואח"כ טומאת מת. וענין טהרת הפרה, כי אפר מורה כמו שאיתא בזוה"ק (וישלח ק"ע.) החילוק שבין עפר לאפר. עפר אית ביה צמיחה ועבידה איבין לעלמא, ואפר לית ביה איבין לעלמא. וזה מורה שאפר מטהר את הטמאים, שבישראל לא שייך שיעדר ממנו החיים ורק עומד ומשבח להשי"ת כמו החי:
records.targetEnglish: Therefore, when one draws from the mystery of wisdom, where no absence applies, he too recognizes that Israel's life cannot be utterly absent. This is why the purification of the red heifer is written before impurity from the dead. The meaning of its purification through ash follows the distinction explained in the holy Zohar between earth and ash: earth supports growth and produces fruit in the world, while ash produces no fruit. The ash's purification of the impure thus teaches that Israel's life cannot be utterly absent; rather, one stands and praises Hashem like the living.
records.themeTitle: Why the substance of apparent loss becomes a means of purification
records.themeSummary: The red heifer exemplifies repair arising at the very point associated with deficiency and death.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef focuses on ash, which seems to have lost even the earth's capacity for growth, yet becomes the means of purification. He locates its meaning in divine wisdom, where the source of life exceeds what human perception can see. This develops the siman's example of the red heifer: the sign of loss itself can reveal a deeper source of restoration.

records.originHebrew: וּמָצִינוּ בַּנְּבִיאִים שֶׁסִּפֵּר הַכָּתוּב כָּל הַמּוֹפְתִים שֶׁעָשָׂה אֵלִיָּהוּ וְשֶׁעָשָׂה אֱלִישָׁע, וְזוּלַת מִשְּׁאָר הַנְּבִיאִים לֹא נִזְכַּר מוֹפְתֵיהֶם. וּכְבָר אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה יד.): נְבוּאָה שֶׁהֻוצְרְכָה לְדוֹרוֹת נִכְתְּבָה, וְשֶׁלֹּא הֻוצְרְכָה לֹא נִכְתְּבָה; וְאִם כֵּן עַל כָּרְחֲךָ אוֹתָם סִפּוּרֵי הַמּוֹפְתִים הֵם צְרִיכִים לְדוֹרוֹת, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיוּ רַק לְפִי שָׁעָה, הֵם פָּתְחוּ שְׁעָרִים בָּזֶה,
records.originEnglish: And we find among the Prophets that Scripture explicitly recorded all the miracles wrought by Elijah and by Elisha, whereas among the other prophets their wonders are not described. And our Sages already taught (Megillah 14a): A prophecy that was necessary for future generations was transcribed, while that which was not needed for posterity was not written down; and if so, perforce those accounts of their miracles are eternally needed for future generations, and even though they were temporary, they opened eternal spiritual gateways in this realm,
records.targetHebrew: והענין בזה, כמו שביאר כבוד אזמו"ר הגה"ק זללה"ה, דהנה יש שני מיני רוח הקודש, יש אשר בא מצד הכנת אדם, שאדם מכין עצמו ומגדיר עצמו בשביל רצון השי"ת ועי"ז בא לידי רוח הקודש. כמו שאיתא במדרש (רבה שיר א) זריזות מביאה לידי נקיות וכו' חסידות מביאה לידי רוח הקודש, והיינו שע"י שהאדם מכין עצמו בכל אלו ההכנות שמחשב המדרש, בא לידי רוח הקודש. וזה הרוח הקודש נקרא נבואה שנצרכה לדורות, כי מאחר שבא ע"י הכנת אדם הוא נשאר בקביעות אצל כל העולם.
records.targetEnglish: The matter is as my holy grandfather explained: there are two kinds of divine inspiration. One comes through a person's preparation: he prepares and disciplines himself for Hashem's will and thereby reaches divine inspiration. As the Midrash teaches, zeal leads to cleanliness, and so forth, and piety leads to divine inspiration. By preparing himself through all the stages enumerated by the Midrash, a person attains divine inspiration. This is called prophecy needed for the generations, for since it came through human preparation, it remains established for the whole world.
records.themeTitle: What remains for later generations
records.themeSummary: A scriptural account can preserve a spiritual opening beyond the immediate event it describes.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef distinguishes an isolated inspiration from a lasting path opened through human preparation. This helps explain the siman's question about recording miracles that served only a particular moment: what remains is not merely the report of a wonder, but an opening in avodas Hashem. The two discussions illuminate that lasting function without making every miracle identical with the prophecy discussed there.

records.originHebrew: עג] כְּשֶׁהָאָדָם מְתַקֵּן מַה שֶּׁחָטָא, אָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַזְמִין לוֹ אוֹתוֹ פֶּרֶק וְאוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם כְּדֵי שֶׁתִּהְיֶה תְּשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל; שֶׁהֲרֵי וַדַּאי יֵשׁ דְּבָרִים שֶׁאָסוּר הָאָדָם לְהָבִיא עַצְמוֹ לִידֵי כָּךְ, כְּמוֹ בְּ"אוֹתָהּ אִשָּׁה, בְּאוֹתוֹ וְכוּלֵי" יַעֲבוֹר עַל אִיסּוּר יִחוּד, רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַזְמִין לוֹ זֶה אוֹ עִנְיָן כַּיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ, וְאֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַזְמִין לוֹ זֶה אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּשֵׁל עוֹד. וּלְכָךְ, כַּאֲשֶׁר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַזְמִין לוֹ, הוּא סִימָן שֶׁכְּבָר נִתְקַן וְנִתְקַבְּלָה תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ.
records.originEnglish: When a person rectifies the flaw wherein he sinned, the Blessed Name arranges for him that exact situation and that exact circumstance so that it constitutes a commensurate, counterbalancing repentance (teshuvat hamishkal); for certainly there are scenarios where it is strictly forbidden for a person to bring himself deliberately into temptation—such as intentionally putting oneself in seclusion with the same woman, which would violate the prohibition of yichud; rather, the Blessed Name providential arranges this or a comparable situation for him, and the Blessed Name orchestrates this only when He foreknows that the person will not stumble again. And therefore, when the Blessed Name orchestrates such an encounter, it is a sign that he has already been spiritually rectified and his repentance has been accepted.
records.targetHebrew: [א] וְעִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא בְּהִרְהוּר הַלֵּב בִּלְבָד, שֶׁהֲרֵי נִקְרָא בְּכָךְ ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״ אֲפִילּוּ הָיָה מִקּוֹדֶם רָשָׁע גָּמוּר, כִּמְבוֹאָר [בְּקִידּוּשִׁין מט:] וַאֲפִילּוּ הַוִּידּוּי דְּבָרִים, אַף עַל גַּב דְּהוּא מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה מִן הַתּוֹרָה, ״וְהִתְוַדּוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר — זֶהוּ מִצְוָה בִּפְנֵי עַצְמָהּ, וְאֵינוֹ מְעַכֵּב הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁעִיקָּרָהּ בַּלֵּב לְבַד, שֶׁמִּתְחָרֵט עַל הֶעָבָר וּמַסְכִּים בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁלֹּא לָשׁוּב עוֹד לְכִסְלָה וְשֶׁלֹּא יֶחֱטָא עוֹד וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּלֹא נִגְלָה לְשׁוּם אָדָם וַאֲפִילּוּ לְמַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת שֶׁאֵין יוֹדְעִים מַה שֶּׁבַּלֵּב, ״קַמֵּי שְׁמַיָּא גַּלְיָא״ וְהוּא נִקְרָא ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״ בֶּאֱמֶת, אֲפִילּוּ הִגְדִּיל עֲבֵירוֹת עַד לְמַעְלָה, דִּ״בְכָל רָשָׁע גָּמוּר״ אֲמָרוּהוּ שָׁם, וַאֲפִילּוּ עָבַר עַל כָּל תּוֹרָה כּוּלָּהּ וּבְבֵית שְׁמוּאֵל וְחֶלְקַת מְחוֹקֵק [בְּאֶבֶן הָעֵזֶר סִימָן לח] כָּתְבוּ דַּאֲפִילּוּ גָּזַל וְלֹא הֶחֱזִיר הַגְּזֵילָה, רַק שֶׁקִּיבֵּל בְּלִבּוֹ לְהַחֲזִיר, מְהַנֵּי וְכֵן מַשְׁמַע [בִּבְרָכוֹת ה:] בְּעוֹבָדָא דְּאַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת דַּנֵּי דְּחַמְרָא, דְּסַגֵּי בְּהָכִי וּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין כה:] בַּחֲזָרָתָן שֶׁל בַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה, הַיְינוּ לְעִנְיַן נֶאֱמָנוּתוֹ לְעָלְמָא, דְּחוֹשְׁשִׁין שֶׁמָּא לֹא שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת וּמְרַמֶּה הַבְּרִיּוֹת, וְצָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּרְאוּ בְּנֵי אָדָם מִמֶּנּוּ מַעֲשֵׂה תְּשׁוּבָה בְּפֹעַל וְהַהַגְדָּרוֹת בַּמּוּתָּר שֶׁהִזְכִּירוּ שָׁם הֵם עֵצוֹת טוֹבוֹת לַשָּׁב, שֶׁלֹּא יִתְקְפֵהוּ יִצְרוֹ לְהַבָּא עוֹד וְעַל כֵּן צָרִיךְ לִגְזוֹר עַצְמוֹ גַּם בַּמּוּתָּר, כְּדֵי לְהַרְחִיקוֹ מֵהָאִיסּוּר שֶׁכְּבָר נִכְשַׁל בּוֹ, וּבְנָקֵל יוּכַל הַיֵּצֶר — אֲשֶׁר כְּבָר קָנָה לוֹ קֵן בְּלִבּוֹ וְנַעֲשָׂה בַּעַל הַבַּיִת — לְהַכְשִׁילוֹ, וְלָכֵן צָרִיךְ לְהַגְדָּרוֹת יְתֵירוֹת
records.targetEnglish: And the essence of teshuvah is in the contemplation of the heart alone — for by it one is called a “complete tzaddik,” even if he was, beforehand, wholly wicked, as is explained in Kiddushin 49b. And even the verbal confession — though it is a positive Torah commandment, “and they shall confess” (Bamidbar 5:7) — that is a mitzvah in its own right, and it does not hold up the teshuvah, whose essence is in the heart alone: that he regrets the past, and resolves in his heart not to return again to his folly, and not to sin again. And although it is not revealed to any person — nor even to the ministering angels, who do not know what is in the heart — “before Heaven it is revealed”; and he is truly called a “complete tzaddik,” even if he multiplied transgressions to the utmost — for they said it there of “any wholly wicked man,” even one who transgressed the entire Torah. And in the Beis Shmuel and Chelkas Mechokek Even HaEzer §38 they wrote that even one who stole and did not return the theft — only that he accepted in his heart to return it — it avails to make him a “tzaddik”; and so it is implied in Berachos 5b in the case of the four hundred jars of wine of Rav Huna, that this acceptance suffices. And what they said in Sanhedrin 25b regarding the “return” of penitents breaking their dice and the like is with respect to his credibility to the public — for we are concerned lest he has not truly repented and is deceiving people, and so people need to see from him an actual act of teshuvah. And the “fences in the permitted” that they mentioned there are good counsels for the penitent, that his inclination not overpower him again in the future; and therefore he must fence himself even in the permitted, so as to distance himself from the prohibition in which he already stumbled — for the inclination, having already made itself a “nest” in his heart and become “master of the house,” can easily trip him, and so he needs extra fences.
records.themeTitle: Inner return and the outward evidence of repair
records.themeSummary: An opportunity to demonstrate repair is distinct from the first truth of repentance in the heart.
records.explanation: Takanat HaShavin separates genuine inward teshuvah from the actions by which other people can safely restore their trust. That distinction explains the evidentiary role of the opportunities described here. They can disclose a repaired will without making an engineered encounter with temptation a requirement of repentance. The present siman explicitly forbids bringing oneself into an otherwise prohibited situation.

records.originEnglish: and as written (Nedarim 81a): "Be heedful of the children of the poor, for from them Torah emerges," for the dwelling place of the Torah is specifically within broken vessels and the bedrock of the Oral Torah was Rabbi Akiva, who stemmed from a family of converts.
records.targetHebrew: ואי' מהאר"י הק' שמשה רבינו היה שורש תושב"כ ורע"ק הי' שורש תושבע"פ. ומטעם זה בא רע"ק מסיסרא ומאשת חבר הקני שבהם הי' ניצוצי בחי' תושבע"פ שסיסרא הי' הקליפה המקפת לקדושה זו.
records.targetEnglish: It is taught in the name of the holy Ari that Moses our teacher was the root of the Written Torah, while Rabbi Akiva was the root of the Oral Torah. records.themeTitle: Rabbi Akiva and the recovery of concealed Torah
records.themeSummary: The Torah's emergence through broken vessels is connected with the release of holiness from concealment.
records.explanation: In Ki Tavo, Rav Tzadok treats the tradition about Rabbi Akiva's ancestry as the emergence of Oral Torah from a place where its holiness had been enclosed. This gives a mechanism for the present siman's striking example of Torah in ‘broken vessels’: the apparent distance of the vessel does not determine the depth of the Torah hidden within it. The passage concerns a spiritual root and does not erase the distinctions in the siman's opening discussion.

records.targetEnglish: And although in Parashat Bo it says, “The people bowed and prostrated themselves,” and Rashi explains that this was over the news of children, while the question there is the wicked son’s “What is this service to you?”—there it is Hashem’s unsolicited promise. Evil does not issue from the Most High, and surely a chain of good will ultimately come from them. So too with Chizkiyahu: “Why concern yourself with the Merciful One’s hidden matters?” Although his son was wicked, to the point of being counted among those without a share in the World to Come, a great chain of righteous people later descended from him, and Mashiach will also be of his descendants. Thus what Hashem gives on His own is certainly good. When a person prays for children, he should pray for worthy children and Torah scholars, through whom the glory of Heaven will be increased, sanctified, and multiplied.
records.themeTitle: The distinction between a divine promise and one's own request
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok revisits the apparent contradiction concerning the birth of children whose future conduct is uncertain.
records.explanation: Poked Akarim returns to precisely the examples that close this siman. It distinguishes Hashem's unsolicited promise, which can include a hidden future chain of good, from the content of a person's prayer, which should ask for worthy children and increased kavod Shamayim. This supplies the distinction left unresolved here between rejoicing at the promise in Bo and Shlomo's prayer that an ultimately harmful request not be granted.

records.originEnglish: The spiritual rectification for anger is change of place, just as the Torah prescribed exile for an unintentional murderer and he was granted a City of Refuge rather than wandering aimlessly forever, for in truth there is the holy 'Fear of Isaac' and sacred Gevurot which are good, in the manner of a young Torah scholar who flares up in holy wrath (Ta'anit 4a), and this is the City of Refuge.
records.targetHebrew: משום שזאת ההגנה הוא רק מצד הבהירות של מ"ר שהיה מנהיר אצלו מפורש כדכתיב אתה הראת לדעת כי ה' הוא האלהים אין עוד מלבדו וכמו שביארו ז"ל במדרש משה המליך את הקב"ה אפילו בחללא דעלמא ומזה נצמח הגנה לההורג בשוגג כי איך היה יכול הגרזן לבקוע את האויר ולהרוג את זה כיון שבאמת אינו נפעל אפילו באויר ובחללא דעלמא שום דבר במקרה ח"ו רק הכל הוא בהשגחה פרטיית
records.targetEnglish: For this protection comes only from the clarity of Moses our teacher, for whom it shone explicitly: “You were shown to know that Hashem is God; there is nothing besides Him.” As the Sages explained in the Midrash, Moses proclaimed the Holy One’s kingship even in the empty space of the world. From this grows protection for the unintentional killer: how could the axe split the air and kill this person, when in truth nothing, even in the air and the empty space of the world, happens by chance, Heaven forbid, but everything is under individual providence?
records.themeTitle: The city of refuge is a place of repair
records.themeSummary: Exile to a city of refuge places a destructive force within a setting that can restrain and repair it.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim relates the cities of refuge to Moshe’s clarity that nothing lies outside divine providence, and concludes that this affords protection even to a very lowly soul. This helps explain why Rav Tzadok specifies a city of refuge rather than endless wandering: the change of place has a positive spiritual content. It is directed toward repair, rather than treating anger as an identity that can never change.

records.targetEnglish: The explanation is: although each soul encompasses all faculties, Hashem, desiring diverse souls, ordained that the composition and blend of faculties not be uniform across all souls; rather, one particular faculty predominates in that soul, coloring the perceptions of all other faculties: by way of example: to one He assigned the hardness of stone as dominant like a heart of stone or stiff-neckedness, to another the might of a lion, and the like. And although all faculties are present within him, their primary lens remains that dominant trait, wherefore perceptions diverge, just as a warrior finds no pleasure in passive rest like a sluggard, and so throughout all details. For Hashem instituted a single order and statute for creation—the order of the Torah (Bereishit Rabbah 1:1), the blueprint of Genesis; and the architectural order decreeing that such-and-such creatures exist in the world must govern the arrangement of souls, which is the ordering of worlds; for corresponding to the diverse faculties within one world is the structure of different worlds, their variation depending upon them.
records.themeTitle: One Torah order, differently composed souls
records.themeSummary: The renewal of souls and the renewal of Torah are related through the same underlying order.
records.explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet explains how different souls can express one divine pattern: each contains the whole range of powers, but a particular power governs their arrangement. This supplies a conceptual basis for the siman’s claim that changes in souls, Torah, and the world correspond. Diversity does not require an independent blueprint for each generation; it can disclose a new arrangement within the Torah’s common order.

records.originEnglish: And this is also the secret of what I heard on the verse "The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable" (Proverbs 10:32): for the holy Ari wrote an efficacious remedy for one whose inclination incites him to a transgression: to utter verbally multiple times the biblical negative prohibition of that sin, whereby the desire will be transformed; and likewise regarding a positive commandment and a good matter.
records.targetHebrew: וּבְיִשְׂרָאֵל גַּם דָּבָר זֶה טוֹב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: ״וַיְפַתּוּהוּ בְּפִיהֶם, וּבִלְשׁוֹנָם יְכַזְּבוּ לוֹ, וְלִבָּם לֹא נָכוֹן עִמּוֹ... וְהוּא רַחוּם יְכַפֵּר עָוֹן״ (תְּהִלִּים ע״ח:ל״ו–ל״ח) וְכִידוּעַ דִּבְרֵי הָרַמְבַּ״ם (פֶּרֶק ב׳ מֵהִלְכוֹת גֵּירוּשִׁין הֲלָכָה כ׳) בְּטַעַם ״כּוֹפִין אוֹתוֹ עַד שֶׁיֹּאמַר: ׳רוֹצֶה אָנִי׳״ דְּמַה שֶּׁבַּלֵּב אֵין רוֹצֶה רַק מִצַּד הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: ״שִׂפְתֵי צַדִּיק — יֵדְעוּן רָצוֹן״ (מִשְׁלֵי י:לב) וְקִבַּלְתִּי הַפֵּירוּשׁ: דְּגַם כְּשֶׁרוֹאֶה שֶׁאֵין רְצוֹן לִבּוֹ עַדַיִין לָזֶה, הַדִּבּוּר בַּפֶּה לְטוֹב שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״שִׂפְתֵי צַדִּיק״ — מוֹעִיל לְלַמֵּד וּלְהַמְשִׁיךְ רָצוֹן לַלֵּב גַּם כֵּן וְחָשַׁב יִצְחָק גַּם עֵשָׂו כֵּן: מֵאַחַר שֶׁרָאָהוּ עַל כָּל פָּנִים מְפַתֶּה בַּפֶּה, עַל זֶה אֲהֵבוֹ — לְהַמְשִׁיכוֹ אֵלָיו לִמְקוֹרוֹ:
records.targetEnglish: In Israel, even this is good, as they said: “They enticed Him with their mouths, and lied to Him with their tongues; their hearts were not firm with Him—but He, being merciful, forgives iniquity.” The Rambam’s explanation of “we compel him until he says, ‘I am willing’” is known: his heart’s refusal comes only from the evil inclination. Of this it says, “The lips of the righteous know favor.” I received the explanation that even when one sees that his heart does not yet want it, good speech with the mouth, called “the lips of the righteous,” helps teach and draw willingness into the heart as well. Yitzchak thought the same was true of Esav: since he saw him at least offering enticement with his mouth, he loved him in order to draw him toward his holy source.
records.themeTitle: Words can teach the heart to want
records.themeSummary: Speaking words of Torah can work upon a will that has not yet caught up with them.
records.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim explicitly interprets the same verse, “The lips of the righteous know favor,” as speech that draws a good will into the heart. This makes the present siman’s counsel more intelligible: repeating a relevant verse is not merely reporting an intention already present. The words can help form the intention, while the distinction between Israel and Esav in the source prevents equating every outward profession with genuine inner repair.

records.originHebrew: קו] "אֵין אָדָם עוֹמֵד עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְשַׁל" (גִּטִּין מג.),
records.originEnglish: "A person does not master words of Torah unless he has stumbled in them" (Gittin 43a),

records.targetHebrew: כִּי שֵׁם בְּכָל מָקוֹם מוֹרֶה עַל עֶצֶם מְכֻוַּן הַדָּבָר הַהוּא, וְעֶצֶם מֹשֶׁה הוּא הַתּוֹרָה, שֶׁקְּרוּיָה "מַתְּנַת חֶלְקוֹ", הוֹרָאַת חֶלְקוֹ שֶׁשַּׁיָּכָה לוֹ. וְיָדוּעַ מִטַּעַם הָאֲרִיזַ״ל עַל לְשׁוֹן רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת ק״א עַמּוּד ב׳): "מֹשֶׁה שַׁפִּיר קָאָמְרַתְּ", שֶׁהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הַדַּעַת שֶׁבְּכָל הַתַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּכָל הַדּוֹרוֹת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל; כִּי נֶפֶשׁ מֹשֶׁה הוּא הַכּוֹלֶלֶת עִנְיַן הַתּוֹרָה כְּלָל. וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (גִּטִּין מ״ג עַמּוּד א׳): אֵין אָדָם עוֹמֵד עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְשַׁל, וְזֶהוּ עִנְיַן נְפִילַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם לַיְאוֹר וְהַמְשָׁכָתוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ. וּבֵאוּר זֶה כַּיָּדוּעַ מִטַּעַם חַכְמֵי הָאֱמֶת, כַּת הַקּוֹדְמִין זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה, כִּי הַתּוֹרָה נָפְלָה בְּגָלוּת מִצְרַיִם, וְהֻצְרְכוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לִגְלוֹת לְשָׁם וּלְהוֹצִיאָהּ מִשָּׁם, וְעַיֵּן שָׁם בָּאֹרֶךְ:
records.targetEnglish: For a name everywhere denotes the essential inner purpose of that entity, and the essence of Moses is the Torah—termed "the gift of his portion," indicating the portion uniquely appertaining to him. And it is known from the teaching of the Arizal on the Talmudic idiom (Shabbat 101b), "Moses, you have spoken well," that Moses is the root of Da'at within every Torah scholar across all generations of Israel; for the soul of Moses comprehensively incorporates the entire reality of the Torah. And the Sages stated (Gittin 43a): "A person does not truly comprehend words of Torah unless he first stumbles over them," which is the mystery of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, falling into the Nile and being drawn out of it. And the explanation of this is known from the masters of esoteric truth, the early kabbalists: that the Torah descended into the exile of Egypt, and the Children of Israel were required to be exiled thither to redeem and extract it from there; see there at length.
records.themeTitle: Torah drawn out of the place of stumbling
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok links Moshe’s name and rescue from the water to the recovery of Torah from concealment.
records.explanation: Ohr Zarua places the teaching about stumbling before attainment within the story of Moshe being drawn from the Nile. Since Moshe embodies the root of Torah, the rescue becomes a model of Torah recovered from exile. This illuminates the siman’s movement from a fall to a newly recovered insight. The sequence describes the repair of a failure; it supplies no instruction to manufacture one.

records.targetEnglish: I will make him a help meet for him. He explained the matter: for such is the will of the Creator, blessed be He, that help and support should flourish for a person from that which opposes him, namely like a disciple to his master, as we find (Bava Metzia 84a) regarding Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish facing Rabbi Yochanan, who would raise twenty-four difficulties against him and he would resolve them with twenty-four solutions, and the teaching was consequently broadened and clarified, and not like Rabbi Elazar who merely told him: 'there is a Baraita that supports you'; for through a person seeing the challenges raised against him, he then fortifies his words with further proofs and his positions emerge thoroughly to light.
records.themeTitle: The opposing colleague can be the essential helper
records.themeSummary: Purity in one area does not remove the need to guard anger toward a challenging colleague.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach reads Reish Lakish’s objections to Rabbi Yochanan as the model of “a help opposite him”: the challenge made the teaching clearer in a way that simple agreement could not. This supplies the positive side of Rav Tzadok’s warning about their quarrel. The person who seems to obstruct one’s Torah may be contributing precisely the scrutiny it needs, so personal anger can destroy an indispensable form of help.

records.originEnglish: Giving charity to the poor is likewise effective to rectify the sin of wasted seed, and generally for anything regarding which our Sages said one is liable to death, charity avails, as written: "and righteousness delivers from death" (Proverbs 10:2; Bava Batra 11a). And for this sin in particular: because through sustaining living souls—our Sages stating there that whoever preserves a single Jewish soul is as though he preserved an entire world—he literally sustains from death the entire universe, including those captive, oppressed souls. Provided that the charity is given to a worthy, upright poor person, for otherwise it does not avail,
records.targetRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 5:2
records.targetHebrew: שֶׁלִּפְעָמִים יִזְדַּמֵּן שֶׁאָדָם מְקַיֵּים מִצְוַת צְדָקָה וְנוֹתֵן לֶעָנִי מַתַּת יָדוֹ, וְאִם יַעֲשֶׂה הֶעָנִי בְּזֶה הַכֹּחַ רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, אָזַי תִּתְבָּרֵר הַמִּצְוָה וְהָיָה מַעֲשֵׂה הַצְּדָקָה שָׁלוֹם, אֲבָל אִם חַס וְשָׁלוֹם יִתֵּן לְעָנִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ הָגוּן, וְיַעֲשֶׂה בְּזֶה הַכֹּחַ הַהֵיפֶךְ מֵרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, יְסַיֵּיעַ בָּזֶה לְעוֹבְרֵי רְצוֹנוֹ, וְזֶה מְכוּנֶּה בְּשֵׁם קְבוּרָה שֶׁטָּמוּן וְגָנוּז הַדָּבָר בְּהֶעְלֵם וְלֹא נוֹדַע תַּכְלִיתָהּ. וְלָזֶה יִתְפַּלֵּל כָּל חָסִיד אֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיַּעֲזוֹר לוֹ בַּעֲשִׂיַּית הַמִּצְוָה, שֶׁיִּזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ עָנִי הָגוּן שֶׁיּוּכַל לְקַיֵּים מִצְוֹתָיו בִּשְׁלֵימוּת, כִּי הָאָדָם מִצַּד תְּפִיסָתוֹ לֹא יוּכַל לְבָרֵר אֶת עַצְמוֹ בָּזֶה, כִּי הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מָלֵא סָפֵק.
records.targetEnglish: For sometimes a person fulfills the commandment of charity, giving a gift from his hand to a poor person. If the poor person uses this strength to fulfill the will of Hashem, blessed be He, the commandment will then be vindicated, and “the work of charity shall be peace.” But if, Heaven forbid, he gives to an unworthy poor person, who uses that strength to act contrary to the will of Hashem, blessed be He, he will thereby be helping those who transgress His will. This is termed “burial,” for the matter is hidden and stored away in concealment, and its ultimate outcome is unknown. For this, every devout person should pray to Hashem, blessed be He, to help him perform the commandment, so that he encounters a worthy poor person and can fulfill His commandments completely. For through his own grasp, a person cannot clarify his conduct in this matter, because this world is full of uncertainty.
records.themeTitle: Praying for charity to reach its proper purpose
records.themeSummary: The life one sustains through charity should become a vehicle for good, but its future use is not fully visible.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov poses the exact difficulty that concludes this siman: the giver cannot know completely how the recipient will use the strength provided. He therefore joins the mitzvah to prayer for a fitting recipient and a good outcome. This deepens the siman’s appeal to divine help without turning uncertainty into a reason to abandon charity.

records.originHebrew: קכט] מִיָּד שֶׁאָדָם רוֹצֶה לָשׁוּב, הֲרֵי הוּא "בָּא לִטָּהֵר", וְהַמִּשְׁפָּט לְסַיֵּיעַ אוֹתוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּיוֹמָא (לח:); וּכְשֶׁמְּסַיְּיעִין, אָז מִמֵּילָא נִיתּוֹסַף בּוֹ רוּחַ טָהֳרָה וְהוּא מוֹסִיף לָבוֹא לִטָּהֵר,
records.originEnglish: The moment a person desires to repent, behold he is "coming to purify himself," and the heavenly rule is to assist him, as written in Yoma 38b; and when they assist him, there is automatically added within him a spirit of purity, prompting him to strive further to purify himself;
records.targetRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 5:6
records.targetHebrew: שָׁאנֵי לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, מַשְׁפִּיעַ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל יָד עַל יָד כְּפִי שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ שְׂאֵת, בִּכְדֵי שֶׁיַּכִּירוּ וְיֵדְעוּ מִי הוּא הַנּוֹתֵן לָהֶם חַיִל וָכֹחַ, וּבְכָל שָׁעָה וָרֶגַע בָּאִים מֵחָדָשׁ אֶל פְּנֵי הָאָדוֹן ה' אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁיַּשְׁפִּיעַ לָהֶם הַשְׁפָּעָה חֲדָשָׁה, וְ"הָיָה טֶרֶם יִקְרָאוּ וַה' יַעֲנֶה" (יְשַׁעְיָהוּ סה, כד); וְזוֹ הַהַשְׁפָּעָה עוֹמֶדֶת לַעֲדֵי עַד, וְאַף לָהֶם יֵחָשֵׁב חֵלֶק וְקִנְיָן בָּזֶה, וְכִדְכְתִיב בְּהוּ: "כִּי חֵלֶק ה' עַמּוֹ", מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁפִּיעַ לָהֶם בְּטוֹבַת עַיִן מְאֹד, שֶׁיֵּחָשֵׁב לָהֶם שֶׁבִּיגִיעַ כַּפֵּיהֶם, הַיְינוּ בִּתְפִלָּתָם, קָנוּ זֹאת.
records.targetEnglish: Different is Israel: Hashem bestows upon them little by little as they are able to bear, so that they recognize and know Who is the One giving them wealth and strength, and at every hour and moment they return anew before the Master, Hashem God of Israel, that He channel unto them a renewed influx, and "before they call, Hashem will answer" (Isaiah 65:24); and this influx endures for all eternity, and unto them too it is accounted as an active share and acquisition, as written of them: "For Hashem's portion is His people", because Hashem bestows upon them with an exceedingly generous eye, so that it be credited to them that through the labor of their hands—namely through their prayer—they acquired this.
records.themeTitle: Receiving fresh help at each step
records.themeSummary: The assistance given to one who begins to return can itself prepare the next request for assistance.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov describes help given gradually, in a measure the recipient can bear, so that the person repeatedly recognizes its Giver and turns to Him anew. This clarifies the ascending movement described here: assistance does not end human participation, but creates the capacity for a further movement toward Hashem. The resulting attainment can still be credited to the person’s prayer and effort.

records.originHebrew: קלב] בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הָעִיקָּר הוּא טָהֳרַת הַלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: רַחֲמָנָא לִבָּא בָּעֵי. וְהַיְינוּ כִּי שָׁם מִשְׁכַּן הַיֵּצֶר וְשָׁם הוּא הַיְגִיעָה.
records.originEnglish: In this world, the primary foundation is the purity of the heart, as stated: the Merciful One desires the heart. And that is because there lies the dwelling place of the evil inclination, and there unfolds the spiritual labor.
records.targetRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:8
records.targetHebrew: וְעִקָּר הוּא וַדַּאי הַתּוֹרָה, כְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (שַׁבָּת שָׁם [י׳ עַמּוּד א׳]): מַנִּיחִים חַיֵּי עוֹלָם וְעוֹסְקִין בְּחַיֵּי שָׁעָה! רַק מִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם זֶה אֱמֶת דִּבְרֵי הָאוֹמֵר שָׁם: דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה לְחוּד [וּדְבָרֵי תְפִלָּה לְחוּד]; כִּי בֶאֱמֶת: "רֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה — יִרְאַת ה'" [תְּהִלִּים קי״א:י׳], וְ"אִי יִרְאַת ה' הִיא אוֹצָרוֹ — אִין" [שַׁבָּת ל״א עַמּוּד ב׳], כִּי יְגִיעָה דְּחַיֵּי שָׁעָה הֲכָנָה לִזְכּוֹת לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם, כְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ד׳ מִשְׁנָה ט״ז): הַתְקֵן עַצְמְךָ בַּפְּרוֹזְדּוֹר וְכוּלֵי, וּ"מִי שֶׁלֹּא טָרַח בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת וְכוּלֵי" [עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ג׳ עַמּוּד א׳].
records.targetEnglish: And the primary focus is certainly Torah, as rebuked in Shabbat (10a): "They abandon eternal life to engage in transient life!"; yet the statement there is also true: there is a time for Torah, and there is a time for prayer; for in truth: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of Hashem" Psalms 111:10, and "if the fear of Hashem is his treasure, yes" (Shabbat 31b), the labor of transient prayer serving as the essential preparation to merit eternal life, as in Avot (4:16): "Prepare yourself in the vestibule," and "he who did not toil on Friday, what shall he eat on the Sabbath?"
records.themeTitle: The preparation that makes lasting wisdom accessible
records.themeSummary: The work of the heart in this world prepares a person to receive a more enduring life of wisdom.
records.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim preserves both sides of the relationship: Torah is eternal life, yet the effort of prayer and yirah remains its necessary preparation. Its reference to preparing in the antechamber explains the siman’s image of the missing outer key. Intellectual attainment alone does not perform the heart’s work of preparing to enter.

records.originHebrew: [קלט] כָּל הַפְּעֻלּוֹת וְהָעֲבוֹדוֹת נִיכָּרִים רַק בַּסּוֹף, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (שַׁבָּת קנג.): אֵיזֶהוּ בֶּן עוֹלָם הַבָּא? "וְאָזְנֶיךָ תִּשְׁמַעְנָה דָבָר מֵאַחֲרֶיךָ וְכוּלֵי" (יְשַׁעְיָה ל, כא);
records.originEnglish: All actions and spiritual labors are recognized only at the end, as written in Shabbat 153a: Who is destined for the World to Come? "And your ears shall hear a word behind you, etc." (Isaiah 30:21);
records.targetHebrew: רָצָה לוֹמַר: שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֲבוֹתָם הָיָה רַק מַאֲמִינִים כְּדֶרֶךְ אָמְרָם: "וֶאֱמוּנָתְךָ בַּלֵּילוֹת", וְלֹא נָגַהּ עֲדַיִן אוֹר הַבֹּקֶר, וְגַם הֵם מַאֲמִינִים בַּלֵּילוֹת, חוֹזְרִים וּמַאֲמִינִים כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל דְּגַם עַל הָאֱמוּנָה צָרִיךְ אֱמוּנָה וְהַשְׁלָכָה עַל "הַשְׁלֵךְ עַל הַשֵּׁם יְהָבְךָ", וּמְקַוִּים תָּמִיד לִישׁוּעָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "קַוֵּה אֶל הַשֵּׁם, חֲזַק [וְיַאֲמֵץ לִבֶּךָ], וְקַוֵּה אֶל הַשֵּׁם" מְקַוִּים וּמִתְחַזְּקִים עַל יְדֵי הַקִּוּוּי שֶׁיִּזְכּוּ לָאוֹר וְאַיִן, וְחוֹזְרִים וּמְקַוִּים, וְאֵין נוֹפְלִים מֵאֱמוּנָתָם
records.targetEnglish: Meaning: even though their forefathers had to rely on faith alone during the dark, as in "and Your faithfulness in the nights" (Psalms 92:3), before the morning light broke, they too believe in the dark, continually renewing their faith. For even regarding faith itself one needs faith, casting all upon "Cast your burden upon Hashem," constantly yearning for salvation: "Wait for Hashem; be strong, and let your heart take courage; yea, wait for Hashem" (Psalms 27:14). They hope and strengthen themselves through their longing to merit the light, and though it has not yet appeared, they hope anew and never fall from their faith.
records.themeTitle: Hope that continues before the answer is visible
records.themeSummary: The final truth of an effort is hidden, so continued reliance on Hashem is itself part of the effort.
records.explanation: Dover Tzedek describes a person hoping, gaining strength through hope, and hoping again while the expected light remains concealed. This develops the siman’s concluding instruction to strengthen prayer: waiting for the end is not passive suspension of choice. The repeated return to Hashem is the form that effort takes when the outcome cannot yet be known.

records.originHebrew: וְכֵן הַדָּבֵק בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁמְּחַשֵּׁב בָּהּ תָּמִיד, כָּל אֵבָרָיו כֵּן, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹף חֲגִיגָה כז.): תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים אֵין אוֹר שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם שׁוֹלֶטֶת בָּהֶן, שֶׁכָּל גּוּפָן אֵשׁ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "הֲלוֹא כֹה דְבָרִי כָּאֵשׁ" (יִרְמְיָה כג, כט).
records.originEnglish: And likewise, one who cleaves to the Torah and contemplates it constantly, all his limbs become transformed into it, as our Sages of blessed memory stated (end of Chagigah 27a): the fire of Gehenna has no dominion over Torah scholars, for their entire body is fire, as it is said: "Is not My word like as fire?" (Jeremiah 23:29).
records.targetHebrew: וּמִיהוּ אֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר, דְּמֵהָא דְּ״הֵם אֵינָן כָּלִין״ אֵין קוּשְׁיָא דְּהָא דְּ״אֵין שׁוֹלֵט״, וְלֹא אָמְרוּ ״דְּאֵין נִכְנָסִים כְּלָל״, מְבוֹאָר דְּנִכְנָסִים רַק שֶׁהָאוּר אֵין שׁוֹלֵט וְכֵן אָמְרוּ [בִּמְנָחוֹת ק׳ רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳] שֶׁגַּם לְמֶלֶךְ שֶׁהוּא תַּלְמִיד חָכָם הוּכַן וְאִם כֵּן עַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּאֵין רָצָה לוֹמַר שֶׁאֵין שׁוֹלֵט כְּלָל שֶׁאֵין מַרְגִּישׁ כְּוִיַּית הָאֵשׁ, דְּאִם כֵּן לְאֵיזֶה צֹרֶךְ נִכְנָסִין וְלָמָּה הוּכַן לוֹ וְגַם אָמְרוּ [חֲגִיגָה ט״ו עַמּוּד ב׳] בְּ״אַחֵר״, דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר הֶעֱלָה עָשָׁן מִקִּבְרוֹ לְדַיָּינֵיהּ, הֲרֵי דְּשָׁלַט בּוֹ הָאֵשׁ אַף שֶׁהָיָה תַּלְמִיד חָכָם וּמֵעִיקָּרָא שֶׁאָמְרוּ ״דְּלָא לְדַיָּינֵיהּ״ בִּשְׁבִיל הַתּוֹרָה, הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא לְהַכְנִיסוֹ כְּלָל בְּגֵיהִנָּם דְּמֵאַחַר שֶׁדָּנוּהוּ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ עוֹלָם הַבָּא, נָתְנוּ לוֹ שְׂכַר תּוֹרָתוֹ שֶׁאֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְקַפֵּחַ שֶׁלֹּא יִדּוֹן וְיִצְטַעֵר כְּלָל בְּצַעַר גֵּיהִנָּם וְרַבִּי מֵאִיר אָמַר לְדוּנּוֹ וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה לוֹ עוֹלָם הַבָּא, וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים חֲזֵינַן דְּשָׁלַט אַף שֶׁכָּל גּוּפוֹ אֵשׁ:
records.targetEnglish: However, one can say that from the statement "they are not consumed" there is no difficulty: for that phrase "has no dominion," rather than stating "they do not enter at all," makes it clear that they enter, only that the fire does not dominate them; and so they stated in Menachos 100a that Topheth was prepared even for a king who is a Torah scholar; and if so, perforce it does not mean that the fire has no effect at all such that he feels no burning, for if so, for what purpose do they enter and why was it prepared for him? And they also related in Chagigah 15b regarding Acher, that Rabbi Meir caused smoke to ascend from his grave to judge him, showing that the fire held dominion over him even though he was a Torah scholar; and initially when the heavenly court ruled not to judge him on account of his Torah, that meant not to bring him into Gehinnom at all, for since they judged that he would have no share in the World to Come, they gave him the reward of his Torah—which the Holy One, blessed be He, does not withhold—that he should not be judged or suffer in the agony of Gehinnom; while Rabbi Meir prayed that he be judged so that he might ultimately enter the World to Come; yet in any event we see that the fire dominated him even though his entire body was fire!
records.themeTitle: Being formed by Torah does not remove accountability
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok’s description of a scholar’s whole body as fire concerns Torah’s enduring hold on the person.
records.explanation: Takanat HaShavin asks explicitly why a scholar whose body is fire can nevertheless undergo judgment, and uses Acher as the difficult example. This qualifies the siman’s account of thought shaping the whole person. Torah’s formative presence is not an automatic exemption from the consequences of misconduct; Rav Tzadok distinguishes entry into judgment from what judgment can ultimately destroy.

records.originHebrew: קנא] עִתּוֹת הַיְּרִידָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָאָדָם שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שׁוּם חֵשֶׁק לְאוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה – זֶהוּ הֲכָנָה לַעֲלִיָּה גְּדוֹלָה, וְהַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי הַצְּעָקָה שֶׁצּוֹעֵק כְּשֶׁמִּתְבּוֹנֵן עַל דְּרָכָיו וְרוֹאֶה שִׁפְלוּתוֹ וִירִידָתוֹ. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַיִּסְעוּ מֵרְפִידִים וַיָּבֹאוּ מִדְבַּר סִינַי" (שְׁמוֹת יט, ב), וְיָדוּעַ דְּרָשַׁת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו.) עַל "רְפִידִים" – שֶׁרָפוּ יְדֵיהֶם מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה;
records.originEnglish: Periods of spiritual descent which a person experiences, wherein he feels no desire for light and divine service, are the preparation for a great ascent. And that is achieved through the heartfelt outcry he raises when he contemplates his ways and beholds his lowliness and descent. As it is written: "And they departed from Rephidim, and came to the wilderness of Sinai" (Exodus 19:2), and known is the exposition of our Sages (Sanhedrin 106a) on Rephidim—that they slackened their hands from words of Torah;
records.targetHebrew: וגם מלמד אותנו איך לבא לחשק כזה ועז"נ ויסעו מרפידים לומר שההפקרות הזה אינו דבר כבד כל כך מיד שנסעו מרפידים שמורה ריפוי ידים מדברי תורה (כמ"ש סנהדרין קו.) ונתנו לבם לזרז עצמם ולבם לבקש רצון השי"ת הבא לטהר מסייעין אותו ובפתיחה פתח כחודו של מחט הקב"ה פותח פתחים שעגלות וקרניות נכנסות בו (כמ"ש שיר השירים ה ב) ועל כן מיד יכולים לבא למדבר סיני שהוא ההפקרות לקבלת התורה.
records.targetEnglish: It also teaches us how to attain such desire. Of this it says, “They journeyed from Rephidim”: this self-abandonment is not so difficult. As soon as they departed Rephidim, which signifies weakening their hands in Torah, and set their hearts to rouse themselves and seek Hashem’s will, the one who comes to purify himself is helped. When he opens an opening as small as the eye of a needle, the Holy One opens entrances through which wagons and carriages can pass. They can therefore immediately reach the wilderness of Sinai, the self-abandonment needed to receive Torah.
records.themeTitle: The departure from weakness begins the ascent
records.themeSummary: A descent becomes preparation for ascent through a renewed cry and movement toward Hashem.
records.explanation: Peri Tzadik returns to the same journey from Rephidim to Sinai and identifies its active turning point: they set their hearts to seek Hashem’s will. This explains the condition within the present siman. Weakness does not improve a person by itself; the recognition of it and the renewed movement for divine help can open a greater readiness for Torah.

records.originHebrew: קנד] כְּשֵׁם שֶׁצָּרִיךְ אָדָם לְהַאֲמִין בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כָּךְ צָרִיךְ אַחַר כָּךְ לְהַאֲמִין בְּעַצְמוֹ. רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר, שֶׁיֵּשׁ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עֵסֶק עִמּוֹ, וְשֶׁאֵינֶנּוּ פּוֹעֵל בָּטֵל שֶׁבֵּין לַיְלָה וְכוּלֵי, וּכְחַיְתוֹ שָׂדֶה שֶׁלְּאַחַר מִיתָתָם נֶאֶבְדוּ וְאֵינָם. רַק צָרִיךְ לְהַאֲמִין כִּי נַפְשׁוֹ מִמְּקוֹר הַחַיִּים יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ, וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְעַנֵּג וּמִשְׁתַּעֲשֵׁעַ בָּהּ כְּשֶׁעוֹשָׂה רְצוֹנוֹ.
records.originEnglish: Just as a person is required to believe in the Blessed Name, so too must he subsequently believe in himself. That is to say, he must believe that the Blessed Name has purposeful dealings with him, and that he is not a pointless creature who sprang up overnight and perishes, or like wild beasts that after death vanish into nothingness. Rather, he must believe that his soul stems from the Source of Life, blessed be His Name, and that the Blessed Name delights and revels in it when it fulfills His will.
records.targetHebrew: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת דַּף פ״ז עַמּוּד א׳) דְּאָמַר לוֹ: "יְשַׁר כֹּחֲךָ שֶׁשִּׁבַּרְתָּ", כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת גַּם שִׁבְרֵי לוּחוֹת מֻנְחִים בָּאָרוֹן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת דַּף ח׳ עַמּוּד ב׳): "הִזָּהֲרוּ בִּזְקֵן שֶׁשָּׁכַח" וְגוֹמֵר, כִּי שְׁנֵיהֶם שָׁוִים בִּקְדֻשָּׁתָן, רַק שֶׁמִּצַּד הַנִּגְלֶה זֶה נִשְׁבַּר וְזֶה שָׁלֵם, אֲבָל מְקוֹמָם שָׁוֶה מַמָּשׁ בָּאָרוֹן.
records.targetEnglish: And our Sages taught (Shabbat 87a) that Hashem told Moses: "More power to you for breaking them", for in truth the broken fragments of the tablets repose side by side within the Ark, matching the rabbinic warning (Berakhot 8b): "Be mindful of an elder who has forgotten his learning through lapse of memory", for both are equal in sanctity, except that in the manifest realm one is broken while the other remains whole, whereas their place within the Ark is identical.
records.themeTitle: The broken tablets still belong in the Ark
records.themeSummary: Believing that Hashem has a purpose for one’s soul is compatible with recognizing one’s brokenness.
records.explanation: Dover Tzedek develops the same approval of Moshe’s breaking the tablets by emphasizing that broken and whole tablets share the Ark’s holiness. This supports the siman’s demand to believe that one’s life matters to Hashem. A visible break does not prove the disappearance of the underlying kedushah; the account calls for renewed fidelity rather than declaring that every present action is right.

records.targetHebrew: אֲבָל יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דִּתַלְיָא בִּפְלוּגְתָּא דְּתַנָּאֵי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה וְרַבִּי מֵאִיר [בְּקִדּוּשִׁין שָׁם] [וְשׁוּב זָכִיתִי וּמָצָאתִי בִּתְשׁוּבוֹת הָרַשְׁבָּ״א [חֵלֶק א׳ סִימָן קכ״ד וְסִימָן רי״ב] שֶׁהֵבִיא גַּם כֵּן לְעִנְיָן זֶה הַךְ פְּלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה וּדְקַיְימָא לָן כְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר מִשּׁוּם דְּדָיֵיק קְרָאֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם וְאַהְנְיַין] דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר הוּא דִּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ דִּלְעוֹלָם נִקְרָאִים ״בְּנֵי אֵל חָי״ (הוֹשֵׁעַ ב:א) אֲבָל רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: דִּכְשֶׁאֵין נוֹהֲגִים מִנְהַג בָּנִים אֵין קְרוּיִם ״בָּנִים״ וּבִתְחִלַּת בִּנְיַן אוּמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית, בִּתְחִלַּת הַשְּׁלִיחוּת לְהוֹצִיאָם מִמִּצְרַיִם נֶאֱמַר בְּפָרָשַׁת שְׁמוֹת: ״בְּנִי בְכֹרִי יִשְׂרָאֵל, שַׁלַּח אֶת בְּנִי וְיַעַבְדֵנִי״ (שְׁמוֹת ד:כב–כג) מְבוֹאָר שֶׁכְּלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל הֵם בָּנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּדְעַל כֵּן הוֹצִיאָם לִהְיוֹת לוֹ לְעַם וּלְעָבְדוֹ לְפִי שֶׁהֵם בָּנָיו
records.targetEnglish: But one can say that this matter depends upon the Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Meir in Kiddushin 36a: and then I merited to find in the Responsa of the Rashba Part I, §124 and §212 who likewise cited for this issue this dispute of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah, and that the halachah follows Rabbi Meir because his textual proofs are more precise, see there, and it brought me great joy; for Rabbi Meir holds that in all circumstances they are termed "children of the Living God" (Hoshea 2:1); but Rabbi Yehudah says: when they do not conduct themselves as children, they are not termed "children." And at the beginning of the formation of the Israelite nation, at the start of the mission to redeem them from Egypt, it is stated in Parashas Shemos: "Israel is My son, My firstborn; send forth My son that he may serve Me" (Shemos 4:22–23); it is clear that the collective of Israel are His children, blessed be He, and that for this reason He brought them forth to be His people and serve Him because they are His children;
records.themeTitle: The enduring root beneath the language of rejection
records.themeSummary: The siman’s concluding verse moves from apparent rejection to the name “children of the living God.”
records.explanation: Takanat HaShavin locates that verse within the dispute concerning whether Israel remains called Hashem’s children when conduct is deficient, and records the support for Rabbi Meir’s view. This explains the depth of the siman’s concluding reversal: the recognition of repair can uncover an enduring relationship, rather than create a wholly unrelated identity after punishment.

records.originHebrew: הַנְּפָשׁוֹת כֻּלָּם קֶשֶׁר אֶחָד, כְּעִנְיַן "יַעֲקֹב חֶבֶל נַחֲלָתוֹ",
records.originEnglish: All souls are bound in one single knot, as in the concept of 'Jacob is the lot/rope of His inheritance' (Deuteronomy 32:9),
records.targetHebrew: אֲבָל בְּפוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, ״יִתַּמּוּ חַטָּאִים״ כְּתִיב, וְלֹא ״חוֹטְאִים״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת י׳ רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳] כִּי שׁוֹרֶשׁ כָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל דְּבוּקִים בֵּאלֹהִים חַיִּים, שֶׁ״חֵלֶק ה׳ עַמּוֹ״ (דְּבָרִים ל״ב:ט׳) וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּקִדּוּשִׁין ל״ו עַמּוּד א׳] דַּאֲפִילּוּ לֵית בְּהוּ הֵימָנוּתָא וּפָלְחֵי לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, דְּיֵאָמֵר לָהֶם ״לֹא עַמִּי״ (הוֹשֵׁעַ ב:א), וּלְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן כְּאִלּוּ אֵינָם עַמּוֹ שֶׁהֵם חֵלֶק ה׳, מַאֲמִינִים בְּנֵי מַאֲמִינִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשַׁבָּת צ״ז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳] וְזֶרַע יַעֲקֹב מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה, שֶׁאֵין בְּלִבָּם אֶלָּא אֶחָד כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּפְסָחִים נ״ו עַמּוּד א׳] דְּהוֹשֵׁעַ קְרָאָם ״לֹא עַמִּי״ בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁאָמְרוּ לוֹ: ״הַחֲלִיפֵם בְּאוּמָּה אַחֶרֶת״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁמּוּבָא [שָׁם פ״ז סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳] שֶׁהָיָה סָבוּר שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לְנַתֵּק שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ הַיַּהֲדוּת עַל יְדֵי רִיבּוּי הַחֲטָאִים חַס וְשָׁלוֹם עַד שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: ״בָּנַי הֵם, בְּנֵי בְּחוּנַי וְכוּלֵיהּ״, וְשֶׁיְּבַקֵּשׁ רַחֲמִים לְבַטֵּל הַגְּזֵירוֹת שֶׁבִּשְׁבִילוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [שָׁם עַמּוּד ב׳] כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר הַצַּדִּיק שֶׁבַּדּוֹר לְמַטָּה מַסְכִּים לְמִדַּת הַדִּין הַמְקַטְרֶגֶת, נִסְתַּתְּמוּ טַעֲנַת מִדַּת הָרַחֲמִים וְנִגְמַר הַדִּין, וּמִצַּד מִדַּת הַדִּין הָיָה כֵּן אֲבָל בְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת מִדַּת הָרַחֲמִים הִשִּׂיג דִּ״בִמְקוֹם אֲשֶׁר יֵאָמֵר [לָהֶם לֹא עַמִּי אַתֶּם יֵאָמֵר לָהֶם בְּנֵי אֵל חָי]״ (הוֹשֵׁעַ ב:א) דְּכַאֲשֶׁר יִתַּמּוּ חַטָּאִים, וּרְשָׁעִים עוֹד אֵינָם, וְנִשְׁאָר הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הַטּוֹב כִּי כָּל חֲטָאֵיהֶם הֵם רַק מִצַּד הַהוֹצֵי וְחוֹחִים הַסּוֹבְבִים לְאָסָא וְשׁוֹשַׁנָּה
records.targetEnglish: But regarding the sinners of Israel, "Let sins cease" is written (Tehillim 104:35), and not "sinners," as they expounded in Berachos 10a; for the root of all the souls of Israel is cleaved unto the Living God, for "the portion of Hashem is His people" (Devarim 32:9); and as they stated in Kiddushin 36a that even when they lack faith and worship idols, where it is said of them "you are not My people" (Hoshea 1:9), appearing outwardly as if they are not His people; in truth they remain the portion of Hashem, believers the descendants of believers, as they stated in Shabbos 97a; and the seed of Yaakov whose bed is complete have in their hearts nothing other than the One, as they stated in Pesachim 56a. For Hoshea designated them "not My people" because when told to prophesy he said: "Exchange them for another nation," as related in Pesachim 87a; because he presumed that it was possible to sever the name of Israel and the root of Judaism through the multitude of sins, God forbid; until the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: "They are My children, the descendants of My beloved ones, Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov," commanding him to plead for mercy to annul the decrees brought about through him, as they related ibid. 87b; for when the leading tzaddik of the generation below consents to the prosecuting Attribute of Judgment, the pleas of the Attribute of Mercy are sealed and judgment is decreed, and from the perspective of strict justice it was indeed so; but through the awakening of the Attribute of Mercy he perceived that "in the place where it was said unto them: 'You are not My people,' it shall be said unto them: 'You are the sons of the living God'" (Hoshea 2:1); that when sins cease, the wicked are no more, and the holy root remains. For all their sins stem merely from the brambles and thorns that encircle the myrtle and the rose (Vayikra Rabbah 23:3);
records.themeTitle: What the unbreakable bond preserves
records.themeSummary: The image of the rope distinguishes injury to Israel’s revealed condition from severance of its root.
records.explanation: Takanat HaShavin reads the same verses in Hoshea as an apparent loss of relationship that cannot eradicate the soul’s root in Hashem. Its distinction between the sin and the sinner explains what the rope image preserves through stretching and division. It also directs the desired outcome toward the removal of sin and recovery of the good root, rather than treating the sin as a model to imitate.

records.originHebrew: [קסו] כְּשֶׁהָאָדָם מְקַבֵּל עַל עַצְמוֹ עוֹל תּוֹרָה וְנִכְנָס תַּחַת עֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, צָרִיךְ קַבָּלָה בַּלֵּב וְהַסְכָּמָה גְּמוּרָה לַעֲזוֹב כָּל חֶמְדּוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַמִּתְנַגְּדִים לִרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
records.originEnglish: When a person accepts upon himself the yoke of Torah and enters under the service of the Blessed Name, he requires an internal acceptance in the heart and complete resolve to abandon all worldly desires that conflict with the will of the Blessed Name,
records.targetHebrew: וְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה הֵם בְּעֶצֶם מְשַׂמְּחֵי לֵב, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (קֹהֶלֶת ז, יט): "הַחָכְמָה תָּעֹז לֶחָכָם", שֶׁנּוֹתְנוֹת בּוֹ עֹז וּתְקִיפוּת, וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא עב:): "לֹא זָכָה – נַעֲשֵׂית וְכוּלֵי", כִּי נוֹלָד בּוֹ עַל יְדֵי חָכְמָה קַלּוּת רֹאשׁ וְנִקְרָא "חָכָם לְהָרַע" חַס וְשָׁלוֹם. וְהַיְינוּ בְּאוֹתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק א הֲלָכָה ב): "נוֹחַ לוֹ שֶׁנֶּהֶפְכָה וְכוּלֵי", אֲבָל סְתָם שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים נ:): "לְעוֹלָם יַעֲסוֹק וְכוּלֵי", וַודַּאי אֵין מוֹלִיד קַלּוּת עַל כָּל פָּנִים. אֲבָל כַּאֲשֶׁר הוּא לִשְׁמָהּ, הַסִּימָן אַדְּרַבָּה, מוֹלִיד יִרְאָה וּזְהִירוּת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין מ:): "גָּדוֹל תַּלְמוּד שֶׁמֵּבִיא לִידֵי מַעֲשֶׂה".
records.targetEnglish: Words of Torah, moreover, intrinsically gladden the heart, as it is written (Ecclesiastes 7:19): "Wisdom strengthens the wise," imbuing him with strength and fortitude, and therefore they taught (Yoma 72b): "If he did not merit, it becomes a potion of death, etc.," because wisdom can engender levity and arrogance within him, and he is termed 'wise to do evil,' Heaven forbid. And this applies to that severe form of study not for its own sake of which our Sages of blessed memory said (Yerushalmi Berakhot 1:2): "'It would have been better for him had his afterbirth turned over, etc.';" whereas for standard learning not for its own sake, concerning which they said (Pesachim 50b): "'A person should always engage in Torah even not for its own sake...'", it certainly does not engender levity at any rate. However, when Torah study is conducted purely for Heaven's sake, the mark is quite the opposite: it brings forth reverence and meticulous care, as they stated (Kiddushin 40b): "Great is study, for it leads directly to action."
records.themeTitle: Imperfect motives differ from contempt for avodah
records.themeSummary: The call to keep learning with mixed motives must be read alongside Torah’s demand for a changed life.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla distinguishes ordinary shelo lishmah from study that produces irreverence, and describes lishmah by its increase of yirah and care in action. This gives a criterion for the tension examined here: a person may begin while the heart is still mixed, but must not turn Torah’s strength into indifference toward serving Hashem. The direction of the learning matters as well as its starting motive.

records.originHebrew: [קסח] הַפְּחָדִים שֶׁל הָאָדָם הוּא מִן הַחֲטָאִים, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ס.), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "פָּחֲדוּ בְצִיּוֹן חַטָּאִים" (יְשַׁעְיָה לג, יד);
records.originEnglish: A person's fears arise from sins, as our Sages stated in Berakhot 60a, and as written: "The sinners in Zion are afraid" (Isaiah 33:14);
records.targetHebrew: וְהֵם אוֹמְרִים שֶׁיִּרְאָה זוֹ הִיא שְׁטוּת, וְאֵינוֹ בָּא מִמָּקוֹם קָדוֹשׁ מֵאַבְרָהָם שֶׁהַיִּרְאָה הַנּוֹלָדָה מִתּוֹךְ הָאַהֲבָה הוּא יִרְאַת אֱמֶת; אֶלָּא מֵאֲבִימֶלֶךְ, שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן יָרֵא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּרֵאשִׁית כ, יא): "אָמַרְתִּי: רַק [אֵין יִרְאַת אֱלֹהִים] וְגוֹמֵר", שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ דְּהָאֱמֶת אֵינוֹ כֵן, וְכֵן הָיָה שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה צָרִיךְ לְשַׁלְּחָם. רַק הָיְתָה יִרְאָה שֶׁל מָרָה שְׁחוֹרָה, וּכְעִנְיַן (יְשַׁעְיָה לג, יד): "פָּחֲדוּ בְצִיּוֹן חַטָּאִים", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּהַנִּזָּקִין (גִּיטִּין נו.): "חַטָּאָה אַתְּ וְכוּלֵי, הַהוּא בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי"; וְהוּא מַדְרֵגַת יִצְחָק שֶׁהוּא הַתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל צַחוּת לְשׁוֹן רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּכָל מָקוֹם: "מֹשֶׁה מִפִּי הַגְּבוּרָה" הַפַּחַד הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה טוֹב.
records.targetEnglish: The scoffers say that this fear is foolishness and does not come from Avraham’s holy source, for fear born from love is true yirah; rather, they say it comes from Avimelech, who was also afraid. As it says, “I said: surely there is no fear of God”—implying that the truth was otherwise, as indeed it was, since he did not need to send them away. But it was a fear of melancholy, like “The sinners in Zion were afraid,” as the Sages said in HaNizakin: “You are a sinner; that is said concerning words of Torah.” This is Yitzchak’s level, which is Torah, as I heard concerning the Sages’ expression “Moshe from the mouth of Gevurah”: the fear that comes from words of Torah is good.
records.themeTitle: The source and direction of fear matter
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok distinguishes a fear of worldly harm from yirah that returns a person to Torah and Hashem.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah contrasts the fear associated with Avimelech with Yitzchak’s yirah, born from love and directed by Torah. This makes the distinction at the end of the siman more precise. The point is not to call every frightening feeling a spiritual attainment, but to identify the fear whose movement is toward Hashem and can itself be joined to joy.

records.originHebrew: אַמְנָם מִדַּת מַלְכוּת הוּא דַּיְיקָא לְהֵיפֶךְ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: אַדָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם – יָדֶיךָ חַדּוֹת וַחֲרוּצוֹת לִרְדּוֹת בָּהֶן עוֹלָמוֹ. וְנֶאֱמַר בּוֹ "אַדְמוֹנִי" כִּבְעֵשָׂו, רַק "עִם יְפֵה עֵינַיִם" – מִדַּעַת סַנְהֶדְרִין (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סג), לְכָךְ זָכָה לְמַלְכוּת.
records.originEnglish: however, the attribute of monarchy is specifically the reverse, as our Sages expounded concerning King David: your hands are sharp and decisive to rule His world with them. And of him it was said "ruddy" as of Esau, only "with beautiful eyes"—meaning with the consent of the Sanhedrin (Bereishit Rabbah 63:8), which is why he merited kingship.
records.targetHebrew: וְהוּא דַּרְגָּא דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ, עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, כַּנּוֹדָע בְּסוֹד ״וַאֲנִי תְפִלָּה״, שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״אַדְמוֹנִי״, וְנֶגֶד אֱדוֹם, שֶׁיָּדָיו גַּם כֵּן חַדּוֹת וַחֲרוּצוֹת לִרְדּוֹת עוֹלָמוֹ, אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵין עוֹשֶׂה אֶלָּא מִדַּעַת סַנְהֶדְרִין (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה, פָּרָשָׁה ס״ג), רָצָה לוֹמַר: הַכֹּל עַל פִּי הַתּוֹרָה. וְהוּא זָכָה דְּ״הַשֵּׁם עִמּוֹ״ — שֶׁהֲלָכָה כְּמוֹתוֹ בְּכָל מָקוֹם (מַסֶּכֶת סַנְהֶדְרִין צ״ג עַמּוּד ב׳), כִּי עַל יְדֵי הַתְּפִלָּה זוֹכֶה לְחָכְמַת הַתּוֹרָה בִּשְׁלֵמוּת.
records.targetEnglish: And this is the high spiritual rung of King David, peace be upon him, as known in the mystical secret of “And I am prayer”, who is described as ruddy (admoni), paralleling the reddish power of Edom, whose hands are likewise sharp and zealous to conquer and dominate his world, except that David acts solely with the authorization of the Sanhedrin (Bereishit Rabbah 63), meaning: everything is conducted strictly according to Torah. And he merited that “Hashem was with him”— meaning the halachah is established in accordance with him everywhere (Sanhedrin 93b), because through heartfelt prayer one merits the wisdom of Torah in its ultimate wholeness.
records.themeTitle: The exception of authority remains governed by Torah
records.themeSummary: The siman’s warning about causing pain must be read together with its carefully delimited discussion of kingship.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla identifies David’s forceful royal role with action only under the direction of the Sanhedrin, and joins that role to prayer for the wisdom of Torah. This clarifies the boundary of the siman’s final exception. A private conviction that one is accomplishing a mitzvah is not the same thing as the accountable authority it describes.

records.targetEnglish: "If he conquers it, well and good; and if not, let him recite the Shema": for within the study of Torah there is an element of spiritual self-elevation and vigor, so that through Torah study a person might feel emboldened in his soul and still fail to arrive at complete, humble clarity regarding his desire; therefore the third test is to recite the Shema ("Hashem is One"), for the essence of the Shema corresponds to what is explained in the Gemara (Ta'anit 31a), that in the future the Holy One, blessed be He, will make a circle-dance (machol) for the righteous— meaning that all will see that everything is equally in the hand of Hashem, blessed be He, and no individual has any superiority or self-exaltation over his fellow, just like a circle which has no head or end; and the unification of the Shema alludes to this complete nullification of self.
records.themeTitle: Shema removes the claim to independent power
records.themeSummary: Recognizing that even one’s capacity to act comes from Hashem can weaken the impulse to act against His will.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains the same counsel to recite Shema as the recognition that everything is in Hashem’s hand and no person possesses independent superiority. This clarifies the practical direction of “know Him” here. Recognizing the source of one’s power is meant to break the autonomous posture of the yetzer, rather than certify the act it is urging.

records.targetEnglish: this occurred later, after the Philistines injected into her the lust for money, mirroring the primeval Serpent; and when they could not seduce her through food or promiscuity, they schemed to corrupt her through monetary greed, the root of all desires; wherefore silver (keseph) shares the root of kisufin, yearning and craving; being the all-inclusive desire through which all worldly acquisitions are obtained. Wherefore even one immersed in another desire is never free from this one; and those who are clean from all other bodily appetites are often not clean from monetary greed; for there are mortals who cherish their money more than their bodies (Pesachim 105a); showing an obsession with money even when it satisfies no physical appetite and harms the body, loving wealth for its own sake; after the manner of "the mouse lying upon gold dinars" (Sanhedrin 29b); this being the root of the Serpent who bites without deriving any pleasure (Koheles Rabbah 10:11 on Koheles 10:11). And therefore through monetary greed comes the ultimate forgetting of Hashem more than through any other appetite;
records.themeTitle: Why a desire for money can be more than a desire for purchases
records.themeSummary: Shuvuel’s attachment to money is treated as a particular power that can be returned to its source.
records.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim explains why money can be desired for itself even when it no longer serves bodily enjoyment: it gathers many forms of longing into one apparently enduring possession. This makes David’s appointment intelligible. The repair is not simply giving Shuvuel enough money to satisfy him, but turning a powerful attachment into responsible service of an entrusted store.

records.targetEnglish: "And Hashem said to Avram: Go for yourself from your land, etc." (Genesis 12:1). It is written (Isaiah 44:3): "For I will pour water upon the thirsty, and streams upon the dry land"; when Avraham our Father, peace be upon him, began to seek and search after the root of his true life, after he understood that all delights of this world cannot be termed authentic life, for all worldly delight serves merely to remove afflictions and impediments; and after all anxieties are eliminated, what is the very substance of life for which the world was created? Concerning this Hashem, blessed be He, said to him: "Go for yourself"—meaning, unto your very self, for in truth, all mundane matters of this world cannot be termed life, and the core of life you will find within yourself: (Isaiah 41:16) "And you shall rejoice in Hashem, and shall glory in the Holy One of Israel"—this is the essence of life.
records.themeTitle: From asking about life to being addressed by Hashem
records.themeSummary: The siman distinguishes recognition of a Creator from recognition of His particular guidance.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach describes Avraham discovering the insufficiency of worldly satisfactions and then receiving the personal call “Go to yourself.” This gives a concrete movement between the two kinds of recognition discussed here: the question arises within reflection on the world, while the answer directs a particular person toward the life Hashem asks of him.

And being part of the House of Israel, they were granted the additional houses of Priesthood and Royalty, which pass by inborn heredity: even a day-old infant of Aaron's seed is a Kohen, and even an unlearned priest stands and offers sacrifices upon the altar, while choice cannot grant this to the greatest non-priest: "and the common man that draws near shall be put to death" Numbers 1:51.
records.themeTitle: A longing for avodah does not itself confer its office
records.themeSummary: The siman allows a broad inward longing while treating its outward expression with yirah.
records.explanation: Ohr Zarua stresses that priestly service is determined by the particular covenant of the priesthood, even where another person is greater in learning. This clarifies why David’s longing for Aharon’s avodah does not by itself authorize performing it. The siman’s freedom of inner yearning must be held together with the actual boundaries of the action desired.

records.targetEnglish: as it is said: "but Esau I hated" (Malachi 1:3), being the polar opposite of the three aforementioned loves; as the Sages expounded on "since you have not hated blood" (Yechezkel 35:6): the blood of the Passover, the blood of circumcision, and the blood of man within his body. And the blood of the Paschal lamb awakens the love of the Blessed Name within the hearts of Israel like water reflecting face to face (Mishlei 27:19); because Hashem passed over and had compassion upon us, Pesach being the festival of love; and the blood of circumcision is the boundary separating Israel from the nations, all gentiles being uncircumcised (Nedarim 31b); this representing the love of Torah in the hearts of Israel who desired it and accepted it; whereas all the nations unto whom Hashem offered it refused to receive it (Avodah Zarah 2b);
records.themeTitle: The three loves expressed through concrete bonds
records.themeSummary: Love of Hashem, Torah, and Israel are distinct expressions of one connected life.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz explicitly returns to three loves and associates the blood of Pesach with Hashem’s compassion, and the covenant of milah with Israel’s willing reception of Torah. These concrete bonds help explain why the siman refuses to reduce love of Torah to intellectual taste or love of Israel to enjoyment of company. Their direction is toward the relationship Hashem establishes and the response it calls forth.
