records.targetEnglish: "His cup" corresponds to the perfection of Wisdom, for drunkenness removes Da'at, rendering a person like a simpleton (Eruvin 65a). Matching Avot (3:17): "Anyone whose wisdom exceeds his deeds... is uprooted," for excessive theory is not true wisdom, matching Proverbs (25:16): "If you find honey, eat only what is sufficient, lest you become sated and vomit it." For excess regurgitates even what was previously internalized, matching: "Give me neither poverty nor riches" (Proverbs 30:8)—meaning excessive intellectual wealth that detaches from reality uproots everything. So too with wine in Berakhot (57a): "There is one who drinks it and it is good for him, and one who drinks it and it is bad for him," for Torah is likened to wine (life for those on the right, poison for those on the left). In moderation, "wine and fragrance sharpen the mind" (Yoma 76b), adding wisdom; but in excess, it removes wisdom and uproots a person entirely. And perfection in Wisdom is that one does not become intoxicated, matching: "Who is wise? He who knows his place" and his true spiritual stature, never overreaching beyond his bounds.
records.themeTitle: Receiving wisdom in the measure one can sustain
records.themeSummary: The example of Ben Zoma distinguishes a powerful desire for wisdom from the capacity to receive it safely.
records.explanation: Dover Tzedek uses the same warning about eating too much honey to explain wisdom pursued beyond one’s proper measure. It defines the wise person here as one who knows his place and level. This adds a needed distinction to the present siman: intensity of love is not the whole of spiritual readiness; wisdom also includes receiving an attainment in a form that one can sustain.

records.originEnglish: All imaginations are born in the heart where thoughts originate, extending thence to the brain, and from the eye, for through sight thoughts enter the heart (Avodah Zarah 20b).
records.targetHebrew: עִנְיַן מְחִיַּת עֲמָלֵק שֶׁנִּצְטַוֵּוינוּ עַל זֶה בְּ"לֹא תִשְׁכָּח", נִלְמָד מִזֶּה שֶׁהַדָּבָר נָקֵל לָבוֹא לִידֵי שִׁכְחָה. שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִיקַּר עֲמָלֵק, שֶׁבָּא עַל יְדֵי רִפּוּי יָדַיִם מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו.) עַל רְפִידִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כָּל הַנֶּחֱשָׁלִים וְגוֹמֵר עָיֵף וְיָגֵעַ וְגוֹמֵר" – פֵּירוּשׁ, בְּלֹא כֹּחַ לְהִתְאַמֵּץ בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה. כְּשֶׁבָּא לִידֵי רִשּׁוּל, אָז תֵּיכֶף גּוֹבֵר כֹּחַ עֲמָלֵק בַּלֵּב, שֶׁהוּא כֹּחַ הַמַּשְׁכִּיחַ מֵאֲמִיתַּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּמַגְבִּיר כָּל מִינֵי דִּמְיוֹנוֹת וְהִרְהוּרִים שֶׁל הֶבֶל וְשֶׁל דִּמְיוֹן שֶׁהֵיפֶךְ הָאֱמֶת. וְדָבָר זֶה נִרְאֶה בְּחוּשׁ, שֶׁתֵּיכֶף עַל יְדֵי רִפּוּי מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה גּוֹבֵר הַדִּמְיוֹן בַּלֵּב, וְלָמַדְנוּ מִזֶּה שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ שֶׁל עֲמָלֵק, שֶׁדַּרְכּוֹ לָבוֹא תֵּיכֶף בְּרִפּוּי מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
records.targetEnglish: The matter of blotting out Amalek, which we were commanded with "do not forget" (Deuteronomy 25:19), we learn from this that the matter is prone to easily slip into forgetfulness. For this is the very essence of Amalek, who attacks due to the slackening of hands from words of Torah, as our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Sanhedrin 106a) concerning Rephidim (from rifui yadayim), and as it is written: "all that were feeble behind you, etc., faint and weary, etc."— meaning lacking the strength to exert oneself vigorously in words of Torah. When one falls into laxity, then immediately the power of Amalek overpowers within the heart, which is the force that causes forgetfulness of the truth of Hashem, blessed be He, and inflates all manner of vain fantasies and illusory musings that run directly contrary to Truth. And this phenomenon is perceived empirically through the senses: that immediately upon slackening from words of Torah, illusion surges in the heart, and we deduce from this that such is the quintessential root of Amalek, whose modus operandi is to strike instantaneously upon the slackening from words of Torah.
records.themeTitle: The loss of remembrance makes room for illusion
records.themeSummary: The siman follows the movement of impressions and imaginations into the heart.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla identifies a linked sequence: weakening engagement with Torah, forgetting the truth of Hashem, and the strengthening of empty imaginings. This explains why the remedy described here is not merely substituting a pleasant image for an unpleasant one. Renewed Torah and remembrance address the loss of orientation that allows the imagination to govern the heart.

records.originHebrew: פֵּירוּשׁ דְּעִיקַּר נִצּוּחַ הַיֵּצֶר עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (סֻכָּה נב:): מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ, וּנְגָעִים וְאָהֳלוֹת הֵם הַיְקָרִים מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּפְסָחִים (נ.) עַל פָּסוּק "יְקָרוֹת וְקִפָּאוֹן" (זְכַרְיָה יד, ו) – שֶׁיְּקָרִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.

records.targetEnglish: for his intrinsic rung was transient life in the union of soul and body, centered in the heart whence issue the forces of life to the limbs, wherein lies moral exertion; for the evil inclination sits at the two gates of the heart (Berakhot 61a), and only "he who conquers in battle is given the daughter of the King—which is prayer" (Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 13); whereas the eternal life of Torah, residing in the brain independent of bodily limitations, is open to all; and on the contrary: "if this repulsive one encounters you, drag him to the study hall" (Sukkah 52b), Torah acting as the antidote to conquer the inclination, studied prior to victory rather than only after it.
records.themeTitle: Torah is also the means of winning the struggle
records.themeSummary: The siman describes the attained clarity of prayer, while Torah also helps a person who is still struggling.
records.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim quotes the same image of the victor receiving prayer, then explicitly contrasts Torah, which is available before victory as the remedy against the yetzer. This keeps the siman’s description of an attained level from closing the path to someone who still experiences distraction. The remedy is already available within the struggle, rather than only after one has overcome it.

records.originHebrew: [רי] כְּשֶׁרוֹצֶה לְכַוֵּין, כָּתַב תַּלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה בִּבְרָכוֹת (פֶּרֶק ה, כה עַמּוּד ב) בְּשֵׁם הַקַּדְמוֹנִים: שֶׁיִּפְשׁוֹט גּוּפוֹ מִנִּשְׁמָתוֹ, עַיֵּין שָׁם, פֵּירוּשׁ כֵּן: לִבּוֹ לְמַעְלָה (יְבָמוֹת קה:). וּבְטוּר וְשֻׁלְחָן עָרוּךְ סִימָן צ"ח נִקְרָא זֶה "הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַגַּשְׁמִיּוּת", וְשֶׁהוּא קָרוֹב לִנְבוּאָה.
records.originEnglish: When seeking to concentrate, Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah in Berakhot (chapter 5) write in the name of the early masters that one should divest his body from his soul, meaning directing his heart on high (Yevamot 105b). And in the Shulchan Arukh (Orach Chayim 98:1) this is termed the "divestment of physical corporeality" (hitpashtut ha-gashmiyut), which borders on prophecy.
records.targetHebrew: וּשְׁנֵי אֵלּוּ הַכֹּחוֹת הֵם כֹּחוֹת נַפְשִׁיּוֹת שֶׁחוּץ לְאֵבְרֵי הַגּוּף הַנִּגְלִים וּמוּרְגָּשִׁים לַגּוּף, כְּמוֹ הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁבַּמֹּחַ שֶׁמּוּרְגֶּשֶׁת לַגּוּף עַל כָּל פָּנִים שֶׁמְּחַשֵּׁב מִצַּד שֶׁהַמֹּחַ גַּם הוּא בְּאֵבְרֵי הַגּוּף וּמִשְׁכַּן הַנְּשָׁמָה וְהַמַּחֲשָׁבָה בּוֹ; אֲבָל אֵלּוּ הַשְּׁנֵי כֹחוֹת הֵם כֹּחוֹת בַּנֶּפֶשׁ חוּץ לַגּוּף, וְהֵם הַנִּקְרָאִים בְּשֻׁלְחָן עָרוּךְ אֹרַח חַיִּים (רֵישׁ סִימָן צ״ח): "הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַגַּשְׁמִיּוּת", שֶׁכַּאֲשֶׁר הוּא מַגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגוֹת שְׁנֵי כֹחוֹת אֵלּוּ, אָז אֵינוֹ מַרְגִּישׁ כְּלָל בְּעִנְיְנֵי גוּפוֹ וְאֵבְרָיו כְּלָל, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן פְּדָת (עֵירוּבִין נ״ד עַמּוּד ב׳) שֶׁקִּיֵּם: "בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד" [מִשְׁלֵי ה׳:י״ט].
records.targetEnglish: And these two sublime faculties are spiritual states operating beyond the physical limbs; unlike mental thought which remains linked to the brain as a physical bodily organ; for these two higher levels transcend the body, termed in the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chayim 98:1) "the stripping away of corporeality" (hitpashtut hagashmiyut); wherein reaching these rungs one loses all physical awareness of the body, as recorded of Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat (Eruvin 54b) who embodied "be you ravished always with her love" Proverbs 5:19.
records.themeTitle: Absorption in Torah and the language of leaving bodily awareness
records.themeSummary: The siman uses “removal of corporeality” for an exceptionally absorbed state of attention.
records.explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet uses the same Shulchan Aruch reference and Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat’s immersion in Torah to explain this language. In its preceding paragraph, the two powers are identified as chayah and yechidah, modes of the soul’s attachment to its source. This clarifies that the discussion concerns the direction and absorption of awareness, rather than a physical separation that one attempts to perform.

records.originHebrew: ריא] תּוֹרָה וּתְפִלָּה צְרִיכִים שְׁנֵיהֶם בְּיַחַד לָאָדָם, וְלֹא גָּרְסֵי אֶלָּא הֵיכָא דִּמְצַלֵּי (מְגִילָּה כט.) וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ (בְּרָכוֹת ח.); וְאָמְרוּ בִּיבָמוֹת (קט:): כָּל הָאוֹמֵר אֵין לִי אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם יָבוֹא לִשְׁכּוֹחַ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִנְיַן הַתְּפִלָּה – הַהַכָּרָה שֶׁהוּא חָסֵר וּמְבַקֵּשׁ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיְּמַלְּאֶנּוּ.
records.originEnglish: Torah and prayer are both required together by man: one should study only where he prays (Megillah 29a) and conversely pray where he studies (Berakhot 8a); and they stated in Yevamot 109b: whoever says he has nothing but Torah does not even possess Torah, for through this he might forget his utter dependence upon Hashem, which is the essence of prayer—the realization that he is deficient, beseeching Hashem to replenish him.

records.targetHebrew: תִּשְׁמַע חֲלוֹם לִפְתֹּר אוֹתוֹ. הַיְינוּ כִּי כָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הֵם כַּחֲלוֹם הַצָּרִיךְ פִּתְרוֹן וּכְמוֹ שֶׁיִּפְתּוֹר לוֹ הָאָדָם כֵּן יָקוּם אֶצְלוֹ, וְהָאָדָם הַמֵּבִין בַּכֹּל כִּי הַכֹּל הוּא רַק מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְרַק מִמּוֹצָא פִיו יִחְיֶה הַכֹּל, זֶה מֵבִין טַעַם בְּכָל דָּבָר וּמַגִּיעַ לְחַיִּים אֲמִיתִּיִּים, כְּמוֹ לֶחֶם הָעִיקָּר הַמְחַיֶּה הַנִּמְצָא בּוֹ הוּא הַמּוֹצָא פִּי הַשֵּׁם וּמִי שֶׁאוֹכֵל פָּשׁוּט כִּבְהֵמָה, אֵינוֹ מַשִּׂיג מֵהַלֶּחֶם רַק חַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְהַמֵּבִין כִּי מוֹצָא פִּי הַשֵּׁם הוּא הַמְחַיֶּה זֶה יַשִּׂיג חַיֵּי עוֹלָם, כִּי לֶחֶם הוּא אוֹתִיּוֹת חֲלֹם הַיְינוּ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ פִּתְרוֹן, וְכֵן הוּא כָּל הֲנָאוֹת, כִּי כָּל הַהֲנָאוֹת וְהַטּוֹבוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם נִמְשָׁלִין לְלֶחֶם.
records.targetEnglish: “You hear a dream, to interpret it.” All the matters of this world are like a dream that needs interpretation; as a person interprets it, so it is established for him. Whoever understands in everything that all comes only from Hashem and all lives only from the utterance of His mouth understands the taste in everything and reaches true life. In bread, for example, its essential life-giving power is the utterance of Hashem’s mouth. One who simply eats like an animal attains from the bread only the life of this world; one who understands that Hashem’s utterance gives life attains eternal life. For lechem, bread, has the same letters as chalom, dream, meaning that it needs interpretation. So it is with all pleasures, for all pleasures and good things in the world are compared to bread.
records.themeTitle: The nourishment is received from the Giver
records.themeSummary: Torah can provide firm nourishment while the recipient continues to recognize dependence on Hashem.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach uses bread to distinguish receiving worldly sustenance from recognizing the divine utterance that gives it life. This sheds light on the siman’s comparison to the manna: a reliable source of nourishment need not produce spiritual self-sufficiency. Recognition of the Giver belongs within the act of receiving and enjoying it.

records.originHebrew: [רטו] הַלֵּב הוּא הַכְּלִי קִבּוּל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּשַׁבָּת (לא.) דְּיִרְאָה הוּא הָאוֹצָר, וּבְיוֹמָא (עב:) עַל פָּסוּק "וְלֶב אָיִן" (מִשְׁלֵי יז, טז) דְּשָׁם הַיִּרְאָה.
records.originEnglish: The heart is the receptive vessel, as written in Shabbat 31a that awe is the treasury, and in Yoma 72b on "and he has no heart" that there resides fear.
records.targetHebrew: וְכֵן כָּל חָכְמָה דְּעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת נִקְרָא: "לָמָּה זֶּה מְחִיר בְּיַד כְּסִיל לִקְנוֹת חָכְמָה וְלֶב אָיִן", שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּיוֹמָא (ע"ב ע"ב) עַל יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם, דְּזֶהוּ רָזָא דִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁזֶּהוּ רַק אֶצְלָם שֶׁהַלֵּב נִמְשָׁךְ אַחַר הַחָכְמָה, וּמִמֵּילָא הַחָכְמָה מְקַבֶּלֶת מִן הַלֵּב וְהֵם אַפִּין בְּאַפִּין, וְאָז יוֹרֶה כַּחֵץ הַהַשְׁפָּעָה, כְּטַעַם מִקֶּשֶׁת שֶׁנִּתַּן לְנֹחַ מִטַּעַם: "כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב וְגוֹמֵר",
records.targetEnglish: And so too all secular wisdom of the heathen nations is termed: "Why is there a price in the hand of a fool to buy wisdom, seeing he has no heart?" which our Sages expounded in Yoma (72b) as referring to the fear of Heaven, which is the mystical secret of Knesset Yisrael, existing exclusively among Israel whose hearts follow their supernal wisdom, whereupon wisdom receives back from the heart and they gaze face-to-face, and then the divine flow shoots forth like an arrow, parallel to the rainbow granted to Noah after "the inclination of the heart is evil from his youth";
records.themeTitle: The receiving heart also gives life to wisdom
records.themeSummary: The heart’s preparation determines whether an increase of wisdom becomes a living attainment.
records.explanation: Dover Tzedek develops the same verse “to acquire wisdom, when there is no heart” as a failure of living connection between mind and heart. The relationship is reciprocal: the heart follows wisdom, while wisdom also receives from the heart. This explains why the present siman treats yirah and peace as more than preliminary restrictions; they form the capacity by which greater wisdom can be received and expressed.

records.originHebrew: [רכ] הָעֵצוֹת לְמַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת וְהִרְהוּרִים הוּא מִצְוַת צִיצִית וּתְפִלִּין, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (סוֹטָה יז.): בִּשְׂכַר "אִם מִחוּט וְעַד שְׂרוֹךְ נַעַל" (בְּרֵאשִׁית יד, כג), זָכוּ בָנָיו לְחוּט שֶׁל תְּכֵלֶת וּרְצוּעָה שֶׁל תְּפִלִּין.
records.originEnglish: The remedies against alien thoughts and musings are the mitzvot of tzitzit and tefillin, as written in Sotah 17a: in reward for Abraham saying "that I will not take a thread nor a shoelatchet" (Genesis 14:23), his children merited the thread of techelet and the strap of tefillin.
records.targetHebrew: והיינו שזה רומז שהשי"ת נתן להם מצות ציצית לישראל, שהן אמת שבשורשם הם מוקפים באורו של השי"ת, אך יען שהשי"ת חפץ בעבודת האדם, על כן הציב השי"ת שפעמים יתכן לאדם פסיעה לבר, ויהיה מקום נסתר אצל האדם, ועל ידי מצות ציצית תוציא יקר מזולל, והיינו שהאדם העובד ד' מוציא אותו מתוך ההסתר ומגיע בחזרה לפני השי"ת, אז יש לו חלק בעבודה והעבודה נקראת על שמו:
records.targetEnglish: This signifies that Hashem gave Israel the commandment of tzitzit. It is true that at their root they are surrounded by His light; nevertheless, because Hashem desires human service, He established the possibility that a person can sometimes step outward and encounter concealment. Through the commandment of tzitzit, “you bring forth the precious from the worthless”: the person serving Hashem brings it out of concealment and returns before Him. He then has a share in the service, and the service is called by his name.
records.themeTitle: Surrounded by holiness and still needing a reminder
records.themeSummary: Tzitzit provides an active reminder rather than a claim that a person can no longer go astray.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains Korach’s all-blue garment as a mistaken inference from the soul’s holy root: if one is already surrounded by divine light, why need the mitzvah? His answer gives substance to the siman’s distinction between erasing every thought and having the power to reject it. The commanded reminder makes return and responsible human effort possible within concealment.

records.originHebrew: אֲבָל מַעֲשֵׂה מֶרְכָּבָה הוּא מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְגַלֶּה לְמִי שֶׁמִּתְעוֹרֵר לוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה מז: הָאָבוֹת הֵן הֵן הַמֶּרְכָּבָה; כִּי מֶרְכֶּבֶת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל הַתַּחְתּוֹנִים בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "הַשָּׂם עָבִים רְכוּבוֹ" (תְּהִלִּים קד, ג), "ה' רֹכֵב עַל עָב קַל" (יְשַׁעְיָה יט, א). וְיָדוּעַ דְּהֶעָבִים הוּא אֵד הָעוֹלֶה מִן הָאָרֶץ לְקַבֵּל שֶׁפַע הַגְּשָׁמִים לְהַשְׁפִּיעַ לָאָרֶץ, וְזֶהוּ הָאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא שֶׁל הַתַּחְתּוֹנִים לְקַבֵּל שִׁפְעוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, עַל זֶה הוּא רְכוּבוֹ.
records.originEnglish: But the Work of the Chariot (Ma'aseh Merkavah) is what the Blessed Name reveals to one who actively awakens toward Him, as written in Bereishit Rabbah 47: the Patriarchs are themselves the Chariot; for Hashem's riding upon lower beings occurs through their spiritual exertion: "Who makes the clouds His chariot" (Psalms 104:3), "Hashem rides upon a swift cloud" (Isaiah 19:1). And it is known that clouds are the vapor rising from the earth to receive rain to water the land, which represents the awakening from below of mortals to receive His blessed influx—upon which He rides.

records.targetEnglish: and see in Shemot Rabbah 15 and Tanchuma, Chayei Sarah 3 on the verse: “Who makes the clouds His chariot”: a king of flesh and blood rides a horse adorned with silver and gold, but the Holy One rides upon clouds. Silver and gold mean love and awe as is known, which are the primary foundation stones and the chariot for royal Rabbis, servants of Hashem, mortal kings; yet Hashem looks not upon these outward adornments alone, rather upon the ultimate culmination—the rung of Jacob, the choicest of Patriarchs, and as I wrote elsewhere, that light and darkness correspond to Abraham and Isaac, and the pillar of cloud to Jacob, and this is not the place to elaborate.
records.themeTitle: Why the divine chariot is associated with clouds
records.themeSummary: The siman distinguishes available intellectual light from a personally prepared dwelling for Hashem’s presence.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah contrasts a king’s silver and gold adornment with Hashem’s chariot of clouds, relating the former to love and fear and the latter to Yaakov’s completed truth. This develops the cloud image used here: the decisive issue is not spiritual display or a forceful isolated middah, but the person’s capacity to become a truthful vehicle for the divine presence.

records.originEnglish: For there is yet a fifth level termed Yechidah, which is the "still small voice" (ibid. 19:12). Meaning that Keter still belongs to the stature of man though beyond his grasp, representing what man achieves through effort with God helping him conquer his inclination.

records.targetEnglish: And in Ra'aya Meheimna (Pinchas 227b) it is explained that these parallel Elijah's vision of the "wind, earthquake, fire, and a still, small voice"; examine it there. The Nogah (translucent glow) represents this aforementioned root; Ezekiel beheld these forces in their chaotic fury during the Babylonian exile, as our Sages expounded: "a stormy wind came out of the north" to subdue the entire world under the hand of Nebuchadnezzar. Elijah, by contrast, beheld them in their rectified state, perceiving that the "still, small voice"—the Nogah surrounding it—is the very Glory of Hashem aligning with His sublime will. And I heard that the "still, small voice" is Hashem's divine seal impressed after human effort (metaphorized by wind, earthquake, and fire); during man's initial striving Hashem is not yet manifestly present, until the still, small voice seals it, revealing that Hashem was immanent within all those efforts in absolute truth; "Voice" is the seal of wind, "silence" is the seal of earthquake, and "thin/subtle" is the seal of fire; mirroring the construction of the Tabernacle, where human labor was categorized as wind, earthquake, and fire, without the Shechinah resting until Moses prayed "May the pleasantness of Hashem...", which was the still, small voice sealing their work with Divine grace; "Hashem our G-d be upon us" is the voice sealing the wind; "establish Thou the work of our hands upon us" is the silence sealing the earthquake; and "the work of our hands establish Thou it" is the subtle quietude sealing the fire, and this clarifies the concept somewhat.
records.themeTitle: The still voice as Hashem’s seal upon human effort
records.themeSummary: The successive movements of spiritual effort culminate in a stillness that is not produced by effort alone.
records.explanation: Dover Tzedek explicitly calls the still, thin voice Hashem’s seal after the wind, earthquake, and fire of human work. Its example is the completed Mishkan, whose labor awaited the revelation of the Shechinah. This explains why the present siman distinguishes even very refined effort from the final mode of union: the final seal confirms the work’s inner truth rather than simply adding another forceful human movement.

records.originEnglish: And afterward "Honor your father and your mother" (Exodus 20:12)—as I heard explained: Father and Mother represent brain and heart, meaning do not reject your own intellect and will either. And this applies after one has traversed all four preceding levels and attained Hashem's aid on Shabbat, whereupon the Holy One leaves him to trial (Section 227) to see if by his own power he remains preserved, which is "Honor." And perhaps it also derives from sweeping (kibbud) the house, meaning cleansing; and literally "honor"—that your intellect and will, which give birth to your active powers, be so purified that of their own accord they align with Hashem's will.

records.targetEnglish: “Take for Me a threefold heifer” corresponds to honoring father and mother. Honoring father and mother is placed beside Shabbos to teach that if a person errs in the clarification of his handiwork, which is called Shabbos, its repair stands beside it: fulfilling the honoring of father and mother, so that he repairs the deficiency implanted in him from birth, from the root of father and mother. How does he repair it? Through the service he performs, he will perceive meaning even at this depth. This is what the sacrificial services signify: a person dedicates all his deeds to Hashem and afterward receives them from the table on high.
records.themeTitle: Kibbud av va’em and repair reaching back to one’s root
records.themeSummary: The siman places honoring parents after Shabbos within a sequence of deeper spiritual refinement.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov likewise reads the adjacency of these commandments as repair reaching beyond one’s present acts toward what was received at birth. This helps explain Rav Tzadok’s extension of the commandment to the mind and heart from which a person’s actions are born. The developmental sequence is directed toward dedicating those actions to Hashem and then receiving them anew as a gift.

records.targetEnglish: Thus I received: the entire world is a book Hashem made. I recall that in my youth I saw a book of positive commandments by HaAdomi, citing a book attributed to Chanoch among the nations, and it seems to me that there was some trace of this there: that all the creatures of the world are forms of letters Hashem engraved in His world, which is His book. The Torah is the explanation He made and composed for that book. These are words of truth, for Torah is an offshoot of the letters of thought themselves, embodied and clothed in the forms of written letters, whereas the world is only a trace and indication. Through Torah one can understand the hints contained in that trace and indication in deeds, corresponding to what is in His thought. Nevertheless, all the deeds and creatures of the entire world form a complete book in which He engraved all the letters of thought in great concealment. No creature or created being fails to indicate a particular matter and meaning in His thought. “He did not create it for emptiness”; everything has a particular purpose, for His praise and to reveal the glory of Heaven. As Rabbi Baruch wrote on “the earth is full of Your acquisitions”: it means how to acquire and apprehend Him, blessed be He.
records.themeTitle: Torah teaches how to read the world’s reminders
records.themeSummary: Created things can awaken awareness of their Creator without their meaning being self-evident.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz describes the world as Hashem’s book and Torah as its explanation. This supplies an important qualification to the siman’s account of encounters that awaken remembrance: the world bears a concealed trace, while Torah teaches how that trace can be understood. Its reminders are therefore joined to learning and the disciplined practice of berachos, rather than arbitrary private interpretations of events.

records.targetEnglish: During sleep, it is possible for the soul to be exchanged, for our Rabbis of blessed memory expounded in Shocher Tov (Psalm 25) on the verse 'They are new every morning, etc.,' that the Holy One, blessed be He, does not exchange souls, inferring from this that an exchange is indeed possible, only that the Holy One, blessed be He, is trustworthy and does not switch deposits entrusted to Him. This applies to one who commits his soul into the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, saying 'Into Your hand I commit, etc.,' but for one who regards everything as chance and nature running its course, it can be exchanged. And they taught (Berakhot 57b): 'Sleep is one-sixtieth of death,' just as after death we maintain (Chagigah 15a): 'If a righteous person merits, he receives his portion and the portion of his peer in Gan Eden; if a wicked person is found guilty, etc.,' so too can it happen during sleep that an exchange occurs where the spark of goodness in the soul of the wicked is transferred to another who merits it, while he absorbs the evil in his counterpart. Concerning this they described the ways of the wicked who would arise early in the morning to pursue evil, etc., whereas conversely it is stated (Berakhot 16b): 'May we awaken and find the yearning of our heart directed toward You, etc.' And this explains what they stated (Sanhedrin 71b): 'Sleep for the wicked is beneficial for them in their way, and beneficial for the world.' The reverse is true for the righteous, for even though he absorbs that good, it is nonetheless deeply entwined with much evil from its original source and requires refinement and rectification; hence it is detrimental for them and detrimental for the world, since he absorbs that good from the creatures of the world during sleep. The remedy for both is the Bedtime Shema and one verse of divine mercy, 'Into Your hand I commit, etc.' (Berakhot 5a), for no evil emanates from Before Him, blessed be He, to any creature in the world, and therefore all will be for the good.
records.themeTitle: Entrusting the night and receiving a renewed morning
records.themeSummary: Sleep can interrupt a fixed pattern of thought and make a renewed beginning possible.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla uses the same Midrash about Hashem faithfully returning the soul and the same prayer to awaken with a heart turned toward Him. It places the night within an act of entrusting oneself to Hashem. This helps explain the siman’s “finding” a new heart: the beginning is received as help, and is then a basis for renewed effort rather than a claim to permanent attainment.

records.originHebrew: וּמֵאַהֲבָה – שֶׁנַּעֲשִׂין כִּזְכִיּוֹת, הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא נִתְבַּטֵּל, רַק שֶׁנִּתְהַפֵּךְ לְטוֹב; זֶהוּ ב' דַּרְגִּין דִּ"לְאִתְהַפְּכָא" וְ"לְאִכַּפְיָא".
records.originEnglish: And repentance out of love—wherein sins are transformed into merits— means that it is not merely nullified, but actually inverted into good; these being the two spiritual levels: 'transformation' (it'hapcha) and 'subjugation' (itkafya).
records.targetHebrew: וְיֵשׁ בָּזֶה שְׁנֵי מִינֵי נִצּוּחִים: אוֹ לְאִתְכַּפְיָא, דֻּגְמַת אֵלִיָּהוּ וּמָשִׁיחַ בֶּן יוֹסֵף; אוֹ לְאִתְהַפְּכָא, דֻּגְמַת מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד, דְּעַל יָדוֹ יִתְלַבֵּן אַחַר הַהֲרִיגָה וּשְׁחִיטָה עַל יְדֵי מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן יוֹסֵף כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל. וְשָׁאוּל, שֶׁהָיְתָה לוֹ הַמַּלְכוּת שְׁאוּלָה, כִּי אֵין זֶה מַדְרֵגָתוֹ בְּעֶצֶם רַק מַדְרֵגַת דָּוִד, חָשַׁב גַּם בָּזֶה לְהִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּכֵלִים שְׁאוּלִים; כִּי מִדָּתוֹ, שֶׁהָיָה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר בְּלֹא חֵטְא כְּלָל, הוּא לְאִתְכַּפְיָא; וְרַק מִדַּת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהֵקִים עֻלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה, הוּא לְאִתְהַפְּכָא; וְכֵן מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד שֶׁיָּבִיא לְתַקֵּן גַּם רִשְׁעֵי כָּל הַדּוֹרוֹת, וְדֶהַחֲטָאִים שֶׁכַּשָּׁנִים כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ [יְשַׁעְיָהוּ א׳:י״ח], עַל יְדֵי דְּיִתְלַבֵּן הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע כְּשֶׁיִּשְׁחֹט וְיוֹצִיא דָּמוֹ וְהָאַדְמוּמִית, וְיִשָּׁאֵר חֲסָדִים טוֹבִים לְעַמּוֹ יִשְׂרָאֵל, כִּי "תַּאֲוַת אָדָם — חַסְדּוֹ" [מִשְׁלֵי י״ט:כ״ב] כַּיָּדוּעַ. וְהוּא חָשַׁב לְהַגְבִּיר מִדַּת הַחֶסֶד דִּקְדֻשָּׁה, שֶׁהוּא הַמְשָׁכַת הַתַּאֲוָה לִמְקוֹרָהּ בִּקְדֻשָּׁה, כְּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ [קִדּוּשִׁין ל׳ עַמּוּד ב׳], הַיְינוּ לַחֲמִידוּ דְאוֹרַיְיתָא; אֲבָל מִצַּד זֶה גָּרַם הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מִדַּת הַחֶסֶד לִהְיוֹת רַחְמָן עַל הָאַכְזָרִים וְלַחְמֹל עַל אֲגָג [שְׁמוּאֵל א ט״ו:ט׳]. וְשָׁאוּל בְּאַחַת וְלֹא עָלְתָה לוֹ, שֶׁנִּדְחָה עַל יְדֵי זֶה מִמַּלְכוּת, דְּנִתְבָּרֵר דְּהִיא שְׁאוּלָה לוֹ וְאֵין זֶה מַדְרֵגָתוֹ, דְּ"מֶלֶךְ בְּמִשְׁפָּט יַעֲמִיד אָרֶץ" [מִשְׁלֵי כ״ט:ד׳]. וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הָיָה גַּם כֵּן אַדְמוֹנִי וְיָדָיו חַדּוֹת וַחֲרוּצוֹת לִרְדּוֹת אוֹתָן שֶׁרָאוּי לִרְדּוֹת, דְּ"עִם יְפֵה עֵינַיִם" [שְׁמוּאֵל א ט״ז:י״ב] שֶׁאֵין עוֹשֶׂה אֶלָּא מִדַּעַת סַנְהֶדְרִין, דְּהָיָה כָּלוּל מִשְּׁנֵי הַהֲפָכִים, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה הָיָה כֹחוֹ לְאִתְהַפְּכָא.
records.targetEnglish: And in this exist two modes of victory: either subjugation (itkafya), like Elijah and Mashiach ben Yosef; or transformation (ithapcha), like Mashiach ben David, through whom all is whitened following the slaying of the impulse by Mashiach ben Yosef. And Saul, whose kingship was borrowed, not being his essential rung but David's, attempted to utilize borrowed spiritual tools; for his personal attribute as a consummate tzaddik without sin was suited strictly for subjugation (itkafya); while the attribute of King David, who raised the yoke of repentance, was suited for transformation (ithapcha); and likewise Mashiach ben David who will rectify the wicked of all generations, turning scarlet sins white as snow when the impulse is slaughtered and drained of its fiery redness, leaving pure lovingkindness for Israel, for "the desire of a man is his kindness" Proverbs 19:22. And Saul sought to elevate the attribute of holy Chesed, drawing desire to its holy source: dragging the impulse to the study hall (Kiddushin 30b) for the love of Torah; but through this he misapplied Chesed into unholy pity upon the cruel, sparing Agag I Samuel 15:9. And Saul stumbled in this single matter and lost his throne, proving kingship was only borrowed by him, for "the king by justice establishes the land" Proverbs 29:4. And King David was likewise ruddy, yet stern to execute justice upon those deserving it, "with beautiful eyes" acting solely with the sanction of the Sanhedrin, synthesizing both opposites, wielding the power of transformation (ithapcha).
records.themeTitle: Transformation includes discernment and restraint
records.themeSummary: Repentance from love is described as a transformation of the power that had been misdirected.
records.explanation: Poked Akarim develops the distinction between subduing and transforming through Shaul and David. David’s capacity includes both opposites, while Shaul’s attempted kindness toward Agag illustrates the danger of placing a real power of kindness where it does not belong. This helps explain why transformation here is more demanding than removing restraints: the recovered power must be directed rightly, with the siman itself retaining a distinction between the prohibited act and the desire that can be returned to holiness.

records.originHebrew: וְהוּא מַלְבּוּשֵׁי גֵּיאוּת דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "ה' מָלָךְ גֵּאוּת לָבֵשׁ" (תְּהִלִּים צג, א). וְכֵן הָאָדָם הַדָּבֵק בְּמִדּוֹתָיו צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת לְבוּשׁ דְּגֵיאוּת, וּבִפְנִימִיּוּת מַכִּיר שִׁפְלוּתוֹ, רַק מִכָּל מָקוֹם בַּלְּבוּשׁ יִהְיֶה כֵּן;
records.originEnglish: and it represents the garments of majesty of Hashem, as it is said: 'Hashem reigns, He is robed in majesty'. And so a person cleaving to His attributes must wear a garment of noble dignity, while inwardly recognizing his own utter lowliness, only that outwardly in his demeanor let it be thus;
records.targetHebrew: וְ"לִפְנֵי כָבוֹד עֲנָוָה" (מִשְׁלֵי טו, לג), דְּתוֹקֶף אוֹר דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָא עֲנָוָה. כְּטַעַם מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, גַּדְלוּתוֹ הָיָה: "וְהָאִישׁ מֹשֶׁה עָנָו [מְאֹד וְגוֹמֵר]" (בַּמִּדְבָּר יב, ג). כִּי גֵּיאוּת הוּא לְבוּשׁוֹ דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "ה' [מָלָךְ] גֵּאוּת לָבֵשׁ" (תְּהִלִּים צג, א), פֵּירוּשׁ: עוֹלַם הָעֲשִׂיָּה וְהַנִּגְלֶה לְעֵין בָּשָׂר וָדָם זֶה נִקְרָא לְבוּשׁ דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כִּלְבוּשׁ הַמְכַסֶּה וּמַסְתִּיר הַגּוּף. וּמִצַּד הַלְּבוּשׁ נִקְרָא הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ "כִּי גָאֹה גָּאָה", שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מְלוּכָה וּמֶמְשָׁלָה נִקְרָא גֵּיאוּת, שֶׁהוּא שַׁלִּיט בַּכֹּל – זֶהוּ גֵּיאוּת וּגְדוּלָּה. וּכְפִי הָאֱמֶת אֵין זֶה אֶלָּא שִׁפְלוּת, כְּטַעַם (הוֹרָיוֹת י רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב): "עַבְדוּת אֲנִי נוֹתֵן לָכֶם", שֶׁזֶּה שֶׁיּוֹרֵד לִשְׁלוֹט בִּפְחוּתִים וּשְׁפֵלִים הוּא שִׁפְלוּת, שֶׁנַּעֲשֶׂה רֹאשׁ לַשּׁוּעָלִים. וְלִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהֵם מַכִּירִים הָאֱמֶת (מְגִילָּה לא.): "בִּמְקוֹם גְּדוּלָּתוֹ שָׁם אַתָּה מוֹצֵא עַנְוְותָנוּתוֹ", "אֲנִי אֶת דַּכָּא [וּשְׁפַל רוּחַ] וְגוֹמֵר" (יְשַׁעְיָה נז, טו). וְכֵן הֵם דְּבוּקִים בּוֹ, תוֹקֶף אוֹרָם הוּא הָעֲנָוָה,
records.targetEnglish: and 'before honor comes humility' (Proverbs 15:33), for the ultimate strength of Israel's light is designated as humility. Reflecting the nature of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, who is the greatest in Israel, whose greatness lay in: 'And the man Moses was exceedingly humble, etc.' (Numbers 12:3). For exalted majesty (ge'ut) is the outward garment of Hashem, blessed be He, as it is written: 'Hashem reigns, He is robed in majesty' (Psalms 93:1); meaning: the World of Action and what is visible to the eyes of flesh and blood, this is termed the garment of Hashem, blessed be He, like a garment that conceals and shrouds the body. And from the perspective of this outer vestment, Hashem is described as 'exceedingly exalted,' for in this physical world, sovereignty and ruling power are termed grandeur, since being sovereign over all is viewed as lofty majesty and greatness. Yet according to ultimate truth, this is nothing other than lowliness, in the spirit of (Horayot 10a): 'Servitude am I conferring upon you,' for one who descends to exercise dominion over lowly, base subjects experiences lowering, becoming a head to foxes. And for the children of Israel, who recognize the inner truth (Megillah 31a): "Wherever you find His greatness, there you find His humility," "I dwell with him that is of a contrite and humble spirit, etc." (Isaiah 57:15). And so they cling unto Him; the supreme force of their light is humility,
records.themeTitle: Outward strength with inward humility
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok distinguishes destructive self-exaltation from the strength needed to enter avodas Hashem.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla explains the image of greatness as a garment, with leadership understood inwardly as service. This supplies a criterion for the difficult distinction in this siman. The useful outward bearing is a means of responsibility and service, while the inner recognition remains humble; self-exaltation that becomes an independent inner claim reproduces the very root of distraction the siman warns against.

records.originHebrew: וְהָאָבוֹת נִקְרְאוּ "אֵיתָנִים" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יא.), שָׁמַעְתִּי פֵּירוּשׁ: עַקְשָׁנִים, פֵּירוּשׁ: שֶׁהָיָה לָהֶם תּוֹקֶף הַחֵשֶׁק בּוֹעֵר כְּאֵשׁ שֶׁלֹּא יִשְׁקוֹט וְיָנוּחַ עַד שֶׁיַּגִּיעַ לְמִלּוּיוֹ: אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּמִדַּת הָאַהֲבָה עַד שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לְתַכְלִית אַהֲבַת ה' שֶׁהוּא בְּהַרְחָקַת כָּל אַהֲבוֹת זוּלָתוֹ;
records.originEnglish: And the Patriarchs are designated 'Eitanim' (enduring/mighty; Rosh Hashanah 11a), and I heard the explanation: stubborn, meaning: they possessed a fierce desire burning like fire which would neither subside nor rest until reaching its complete fulfillment: Abraham our father, peace be upon him, in the attribute of love, until he arrived at the ultimate love of Hashem, which entails distancing all loves other than Him;
records.targetHebrew: כִּי הַג׳ אָבוֹת הֵם שׁוֹרֶשׁ לְג׳ קְדוּשׁוֹת הַנַּזְכָּרוֹת: אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״תְּחִלָּה לַגֵּרִים״ (חֲגִיגָה ג׳ עַמּוּד א׳) — הוּא הַתְחָלַת הַקְּדוּשָׁה שֶׁמִּלְּמַטָּה בְּהַגְדָּרַת כָּל אֵבָרָיו וְכֹחוֹתָיו לִהְיוֹת הַכֹּל בִּקְדוּשָׁה וְהוּא הוּצְרַךְ לְקָרֵב אֶת עַצְמוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (ע׳ סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳): ״דִּבְגֵרִים תְּחִלָּה: ׳וְהָיוּ לִי לְעָם׳״ וְנִתְנַסָּה בְּי׳ (עֲשָׂרָה) נִסְיוֹנוֹת לְהִתְבָּרֵר בְּי׳ מַדְרֵיגוֹת שֶׁל כָּל קוֹמָה מִצַּד קְדֻשַּׁת עַצְמוֹ שֶׁמִּלְּמַטָּה בְּמִלְחֶמֶת הַיֵּצֶר. כִּי כָל נִסָּיוֹן עַל כָּרְחָךְ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ יֵצֶר הָרוֹבֵץ וּמַסִּית וְהוּא צָרִיךְ לְהִתְגַּבֵּר נֶגְדּוֹ, דְּאִם כְּבָר יִצְרוֹ בְּיָדוֹ — אֵין כָּאן נִסָּיוֹן
records.targetEnglish: For the three Patriarchs are the living root of these three holinesses: Abraham our father, the first of converts (Chagigah 3a), is the inception of holiness from below, fencing all his organs to be holy; having to draw himself near, converts being accepted initially through human initiative; tested with Ten Trials (Avos 5:3) to refine the ten rungs of human stature through his war against the yetzer. For every trial requires an inciting yetzer whom man must conquer, for if the yetzer is already tamed, no trial exists;
records.themeTitle: The presence of struggle is not the absence of a holy task
records.themeSummary: Human longing has both good and dangerous possibilities, so greatness is not measured by the absence of conflict alone.
records.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim describes Avraham’s tests as the clarification of the full range of his powers, and states that an actual test requires an opposing impulse to overcome. This clarifies the present siman’s claim about the human advantage over angels. The power that makes willing service possible also makes struggle possible; what determines its direction is the work of bringing it into kedushah.

records.originHebrew: רנב] הָאָדָם צָרִיךְ לְהַכִּיר כִּי הַחֵשֶׁק וּנְדִיבוּת לֵב שֶׁלּוֹ הוּא גַּם כֵּן מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה ה, ב): "הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּנִדְבַת בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ: "כִּי מִמְּךָ הַכֹּל וּמִיָּדְךָ וְגוֹמֵר", "וּלְךָ הַכֹּל" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א כט, יד). וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה הַחֵשֶׁק הַהוּא נִקְבָּע בַּלֵּב שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כֵּן תָּמִיד. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁבִּיקֵּשׁ שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ: "שָׁמְרָה זֹּאת לְעוֹלָם וְגוֹמֵר" (שָׁם, יח), דְּמֵאַחַר שֶׁהַכֹּל מִמְּךָ וְאַתָּה נִצְחִי וְאֵינְךָ מִשְׁתַּנֶּה, תּוּכַל לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן יֵצֶר לְבַב עַמְּךָ וְחֶשְׁקָם לְעוֹלָם.
records.originEnglish: A person must recognize that his desire and generosity of heart likewise derive from Hashem, blessed be He, as it is written (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2): 'The Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel', and as King David, peace be upon him, proclaimed at the donation for the Temple: 'For all things come from You, and of Your own have we given You, etc.' And through this realization, that desire becomes permanently fixed in the heart to endure always. And as he pleaded there afterward: 'Keep this forever, etc.' (ibid. 18), for since everything is from You and You are eternal and immutable, You can preserve thus the inner inclination of Your people's heart and their desire forever.
records.targetHebrew: והכרה היותר גדולה יש לו לאדם בהראשית, ששם מכיר מפורש שכל כח הצמיחה הוא מן השי"ת. ולזה ציותה התורה, ולקחת מראשית כל פרי האדמה, כי במקום שאדם מכיר שהניח לו השי"ת מקום להכיר, כי ממך הכל, שם צריך האדם להחזירו להשי"ת.
records.targetEnglish: A person has the clearest recognition in the first produce, for there he recognizes explicitly that the entire power of growth comes from Hashem. The Torah therefore commanded, “You shall take from the first of all the fruit of the ground”: in the place where a person recognizes that Hashem has left him an opening to recognize “everything comes from You,” there he must return it to Hashem.
records.themeTitle: Returning the gift at the point of first recognition
records.themeSummary: Acknowledging the source of generosity is part of making that generosity an enduring possession.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef applies the same verse “everything comes from You” to the first fruits, before possession and habit obscure the source of their growth. The gift is returned at the moment its dependence is clearest. This illuminates why the present siman begins by returning even the generous impulse to Hashem: that recognition is part of acquiring a lasting relation to the good, rather than merely surrendering ownership of it.

records.originHebrew: אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל מִצְוָה פְּרָטִית הִיא עוֹנֶג פְּרָטִי, וְהֲגַם שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הֲבָנַת סוֹדוֹת הַמִּצְווֹת יוּכַל לָדַעַת סוֹד כָּל מִצְוָה פְּרָטִית בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ, הָעוֹנֶג מִזֶּה הוּא מִצַּד יְדִיעַת הַסּוֹד וְהוּא בִּכְלַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וּבְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה וַדַּאי יֵשׁ עוֹנֶג פְּרָטִי מֵעֶצֶם אוֹתוֹ חִידּוּשׁ דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא, וּבְכָל חִידּוּשׁ פְּרָטִי עוֹנֶג פְּרָטִי.
records.originEnglish: Yet in truth every specific mitzvah contains an individualized delight, and although by understanding the mystical secrets of the mitzvot one can grasp the secret of each individually, the delight from that stems from knowing the secret, which falls under Torah study; and in words of Torah there is certainly specific delight from each individual novel insight, and in every specific innovation, a distinct delight.

records.targetEnglish: For in this world Hashem, blessed be He, concealed the depth of intention hidden in the performance of the commandments. If a commandment consisted solely of its intention, why, then, did Hashem, blessed be He, command its actual performance? This shows that a person does not know the Torah concealed and hidden in the performance of the commandments in this world. As stated in the Talmud (Sotah 21a): Rav Yosef said: “A commandment, while one engages in it, protects and saves; when one is not engaging in it, it protects, but does not save.” That is, when he is no longer engaged in it, none of the commandment’s holiness remains in his body, because the body does not understand its root. But regarding a commandment belonging to a person, especially if he devotes himself extensively to its details and understanding, Hashem, blessed be He, will illuminate it for him, so that he understands the commandment through the light of Torah, such that the commandment’s entire essence becomes words of Torah. He will understand its intention, and see that the commandment’s outward form and action belong only to this world.
records.themeTitle: The act can contain more than the doer presently understands
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the soul’s garments of action from the inward nourishment received through understanding.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov likewise explains why the deed of a mitzvah cannot be replaced by its presently understood intention: its inner Torah is still concealed. When that inner meaning is illuminated, the mitzvah can be apprehended as Torah. This clarifies the siman’s distinction between a general joy in fulfilling Hashem’s will and the particular delight disclosed through a mitzvah’s inner meaning.

records.originHebrew: וְהַכֹּהֵן הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁנִּכְנָס לְקָדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים, דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְגַלֶּה לוֹ סְתָרָיו וְסוֹד ה', דְּלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא יח.) דְּצָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה גָּדוֹל בְּחָכְמָה, הוּא הַלּוֹבֵשׁ מַחֲלָצוֹת כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל. וְהֵם ד' בְּגָדִים הַנּוֹסָפִים שֶׁהֵם לְעוּמַּת ד' הַנִּזְכָּר, רַק שֶׁהֵם מַחֲלָצוֹת וְסוּדְרָא דְּרַבָּנַן:
records.originEnglish: And the High Priest who enters the Holy of Holies, wherein Hashem reveals to him His hidden matters and supernal secret, wherefore they taught (Yoma 18a) that he must be great in wisdom, he is the one who dons the translucent robes (machalatzot) as mentioned above. And these are the four additional golden garments corresponding to the aforementioned four, except that they are machalatzot and the scholars' sudara:
records.targetHebrew: וזהו נמי שהעבודה של כהן גדול בכל השנה היה בבגדי זהב היינו שהיה מנהיר בעבודתו בכל הלבושים את אור רצונו ית' אכן ביוה"כ שנכנס לפני ולפנים והשי"ת מראה מפורש את אור רצונו בלי שום לבוש לכן לא יתיצב אז נוכח השי"ת הכה"ג בשום לבוש והתפשטות רק בבגדי בד להורות שמוסר הכלי קיבול נמי אז להשי"ת.
records.targetEnglish: This is also why the High Priest’s service throughout the year was in golden garments: through his service he illuminated all the garments with the light of Hashem’s will. But on Yom Kippur, when he enters the innermost place and Hashem reveals the light of His will explicitly without any garment, the High Priest does not then stand before Hashem in such garments and expansion, but in linen garments, indicating that he then surrenders even the receiving vessel to Hashem.
records.themeTitle: Garments that reveal, and the linen garments of inward entry
records.themeSummary: The symbolic account of the High Priest’s garments distinguishes different forms of revealing the inward life.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim contrasts the golden garments that reveal divine light throughout the forms of worldly service with the linen garments of the inward Yom Kippur entry. This clarifies the register of the siman’s symbolism: its account of the eight garments is not a statement that all eight are worn in the innermost entry. The contrast also explains how a garment can reveal inward meaning while a further stage expresses the surrender of the receiving vessel itself.

records.originHebrew: הַכְּנִיסָה לָרַע הוּא עַל יְדֵי לֵיצָנוּת, כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּיוֹמָא (לח:): "הַבָּא לִיטַּמֵּא פּוֹתְחִין [לוֹ]", מִקְּרָא דְּ"אִם לַלֵּצִים הוּא יָלִיץ" (מִשְׁלֵי ג, לד);
records.originEnglish: The entryway into evil is through mockery, as our Sages taught in Yoma (38b): “To one who comes to defile himself, they open the door,” derived from the verse: “If it concerns the scorners, he scoffs”;
records.targetHebrew: אֲבָל חָכְמָה חִיצוֹנִית הַמְּצוּיָה גַּם בְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם וְיֵשׁ מַה שֶּׁהוּא נִקְרָא ״חָכְמָה״ בֶּאֱמֶת שֶׁנִּקְרָא גַּם בִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב חָכְמָה אֶלָּא שֶׁהֵם קוֹלְטִים הַפְּסֹולֶת מִמֶּנּוּ כִּי בָּזֶה שָׁרְשָׁם, וּפְסֹולְתּוֹ הִיא הַלֵּיצָנוּת מֵחָכְמָה הָאֲמִיתִּית וְכָל מִינֵי עֲבוֹדוֹת זָרוֹת שֶׁהָיוּ מַתְעִים הַהֲמוֹן, וַדַּאי הָיוּ מַרְאִים לָהֶם בְּחָכְמָתָם הַמְזוֹהֶמֶת שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ מַמָּשׁ אֲבָל הַכֹּל נִמְשָׁךְ מִצַּד הַלֵּיצָנוּת מֵהָאֱמֶת, עַל יְדֵי זֶה מַמְצִיאִים שֶׁקֶר הַמִּתְדַּמֶּה לֶאֱמֶת וְזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן עִנְיַן עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דִּפְעוֹר דִּלְעֻומַּת זֶה נִקְבַּר מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁנִּקְרֵאת עַל שְׁמוֹ שֶׁהוּא מַמָּשׁ הֵיפֶךְ הַלֵּיצָנוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: ״נִכְנַס דְּבַר שֶׁל תּוֹרָה — יָצָא כְּנֶגְדּוֹ דְּבַר שֶׁל לֵיצָנוּת״ (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה א:ב)
records.targetEnglish: but external wisdom found among the nations of the world, and there is that which is genuinely termed "wisdom" even in the language of Scripture, yet they absorb the dross from it, such being their root, and its dross is mockery of true sacred wisdom; and in all pagan idolatries that misled the masses, they demonstrated through their corrupted intellect that it supposedly held substance, yet all of it derived from cynicism toward the truth, forging a falsehood that mimics the truth. And this is likewise the nature of the idolatry of Ba'al Pe'or (Bamidbar 25:3); directly opposite which Moshe Rabbeinu was buried, he being the root of the Torah called by his name (Malachi 3:22), which is the exact antithesis of mockery, as written: "when a word of Torah enters, a word of scoffing departs" (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:2);
records.themeTitle: Mockery can manufacture a false substitute for truth
records.themeSummary: The opening of the final siman treats mockery as a gateway into other forms of estrangement.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz describes the progression from mocking true wisdom to constructing a false appearance of truth. This explains why the present siman gives leitzanus a foundational role, rather than counting it as just another isolated bad habit. Once the mind dismisses the very standard by which it could be corrected, it becomes able to justify a substitute on its own terms.

records.originHebrew: אֲבָל כֶּתֶר הוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם וּכְמוֹ מַקִּיף כַּנּוֹדָע, וְהוּא בָּרַע כָּל מִינֵי מַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת הַנִּכְנָסוֹת וּפוֹרְחוֹת מֵעַצְמָן לַמּוֹחַ וּמְבַלְבְּלִים. וְשָׁרְשָׁן מִקְּלִיפַּת נוֹגַהּ שֶׁמִּכֹּחוֹ כָּל דִּבְרֵי הָרְשׁוּת כַּנּוֹדָע, וְזֶה עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ וּמַשְׁכָּא דְּחִוְיָא, דְּיָדוּעַ דְּהוּא מִקְּלִיפַּת נוֹגַהּ וְהוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַחֶמְדָּה הַגּוּפָנִית, שֶׁזֶּה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְתַקֵּן לְגַמְרֵי בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, כִּי עַל יְדֵי תִּיקּוּנָהּ הוּא בִּילּוּעַ הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח שֶׁהוּא מִכֹּחַ עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ.
records.originEnglish: However, Keter is the concealed root and acts as an encompassing light (makif), and in evil this reflects all extraneous thoughts that enter and flit spontaneously into the brain, causing confusion. And their root is in Kelipat Nogah from whose force stem all discretionary worldly matters, and this is the counsel of the serpent and the serpent's skin, which is known to originate from Kelipat Nogah, and is the root of bodily lust, which is impossible to rectify completely in this world, for through its complete rectification comes the swallowing up of death forever, which derives from the serpent's counsel.

records.targetEnglish: “When God destroyed the cities of the plain, God remembered Avraham and sent Lot out of the overthrow.” The connection between remembering Avraham and rescuing Lot is explained in the holy Zohar, Lech Lecha, page 80: the evil inclination is named Lot, and Avraham is the soul. The writings of the Ari explain that Lot is from kelipas nogah, a mixture of good and evil, as it says, “and a brightness around it”: it is darkness with the light encamping around it. The soul’s principal coming into this world is to clarify this kelipah and raise it to the highest heights. This means that kelipas nogah signifies all permitted, optional matters. Although they are entirely permitted, they still require clarification, as the Sages said, “Sanctify yourself in what is permitted to you.”
records.themeTitle: Permitted life still has a work of refinement
records.themeSummary: The closing discussion distinguishes overt transgression from the mixture involved in ordinary permitted life.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov identifies kelipas nogah with permitted matters that nevertheless require clarification, through the example of Lot’s rescue for Avraham’s sake. This helps explain why the final siman still speaks of repair after discussing the rejection of open evil. The remaining task concerns the direction and use of permitted powers, not a claim that everything permitted is already a transgression.
